cards.q: Why is an object more than a dictionary of values?
cards.a: Because the operations travel with the data. Anything holding the object also holds the only code allowed to change it, so the rules cannot be bypassed.

cards.q: What does it mean to say two variables reference the same object?
cards.a: Both names hold the same address, so there is only one object. A change made through either name is visible through both.

cards.q: What is the difference between identity and equality?
cards.a: Identity asks whether two names point at the *same* object. Equality asks whether two objects hold the same values. Two different objects can be equal.

practice.q: Explain the relationship between a class and an object, using an example.
points: A class is a definition or blueprint stating what attributes and methods objects of that kind have.
An object is a specific instance created from that class at run time.
Each object has its own values for the attributes, so two objects of the same class can differ.
A valid example is given, such as a Student class with objects for individual students.

practice.q: State what a constructor is and explain why it is useful.
points: A constructor is a method that runs automatically when an object is created.
It assigns initial values to the object's attributes.
This guarantees the object is in a valid state before any other code can use it.

practice.q: Distinguish between an instance variable and a class variable, giving a use for each.
points: An instance variable belongs to a single object, and each object has its own copy.
A class variable is shared by every object of the class.
An instance variable suits data that differs per object, such as a student's name.
A class variable suits data common to all objects, such as a count of how many have been created.

practice.q: Explain what is meant by `self` in a method definition and why it is needed.
points: `self` refers to the particular object on which the method was called.
Methods are stored once with the class rather than copied into each object.
The parameter therefore tells the method which object's data to work on.
Without it, an assignment inside the method would create a local variable rather than change the object.

practice.q: A program creates two objects of the same class and changes an attribute of one. Explain why the other is unaffected, and state one case in which it would be affected.
points: Each object has its own memory holding its own instance variables.
Assigning to one object's attribute writes only to that object's storage.
If the attribute were a class variable, it would be shared and both would change.
The same happens if both names reference the same single object rather than two objects.

practice.q: A student writes a program using two parallel lists, one of names and one of marks, and is told to rewrite it using objects. Discuss the advantages of doing so.
points: Related data is held together in one object rather than spread across separate lists.
It becomes impossible for the lists to fall out of step, which is a common source of bugs.
Operations on a student, such as calculating a grade, can be methods on the object rather than loose functions.
Adding a further field requires changing one class rather than every place a list is indexed.
The program reads in terms of the problem — students and marks — rather than in terms of indices.

practice.q: Explain the difference between testing identity and testing equality for objects, and give a situation where the distinction matters.
points: Identity tests whether two references point to the same object in memory.
Equality tests whether two objects hold values that are considered the same.
Two distinct objects can be equal, so an identity test would wrongly report them as different.
It matters when, for example, checking whether a student appears twice in a list, where equality of the data is what is wanted.

pages.title: Encapsulation and interfaces
pages.lede: Why hiding data is not about secrecy, what an invariant is, and how to tell a useful getter from a pointless one.

cards.a: Keeping an object's data private and exposing only methods, so the object's state can only be changed in ways the class allows.
Accessible from anywhere. Anything public is a promise you must keep working, because other code now depends on it.
Accessible only from inside the class. It can be renamed, retyped or removed without breaking any other code.
Accessible from inside the class and from its subclasses, but not from unrelated code.

cards.q: What is an accessor, or getter?
cards.a: A method that returns the value of a private attribute without allowing it to be changed.

cards.q: What is a mutator, or setter?
cards.a: A method that changes a private attribute, and which can validate the new value before accepting it.
A statement about an object that must be true at all times, such as a balance never being negative. Encapsulation is how it is enforced.
Validation happens in one place so bad state cannot be created, and the internal representation can be changed without altering any calling code.

cards.q: What is an interface, in object-oriented terms?
cards.a: The set of public methods an object offers — what it can be asked to do, with nothing said about how it does it.

cards.q: Why is a getter-and-setter pair for every attribute a poor design?
cards.a: Because it exposes the same state under a longer name. Nothing is protected and the class has no rules of its own.
By convention. A leading underscore means "internal", and a double underscore triggers name mangling, but neither is enforced by the language.

cards.q: What does information hiding buy you when a program changes?
cards.a: Anything hidden can be rewritten freely. Only what was exposed constrains you, so a small public interface keeps future options open.

practice.q: Explain what encapsulation is and state two benefits of it.
points: Encapsulation means keeping an object's data private and providing access only through its methods.
Any change to the state must pass through code the class controls.
Validation can therefore be written once and cannot be bypassed.
The internal representation can be changed without affecting code that uses the object.

practice.q: Describe the difference between public, private and protected access.
points: Public members can be accessed from anywhere in the program.
Private members can be accessed only from within the class that defines them.
Protected members can be accessed within the class and its subclasses, but not from unrelated code.

practice.q: A class stores a bank balance as a public attribute. Explain the risks and describe how encapsulation would remove them.
points: Any code anywhere can assign to the balance, including invalid values such as a negative amount.
A wrong value could originate anywhere in the program, making the fault hard to locate.
Making the attribute private and providing deposit and withdraw methods forces all changes through one place.
Those methods can reject invalid amounts, so the object can never enter an invalid state.

practice.q: Explain what is meant by an invariant, and how a class maintains one.
points: An invariant is a condition about an object's state that must always hold.
The constructor establishes it when the object is created.
Every method that changes the state must leave it true, rejecting changes that would break it.
This is only possible if the state cannot be changed from outside the class.

practice.q: A student adds a getter and a setter for every private attribute in a class. Discuss whether this achieves encapsulation.
points: The attributes are technically private, so the syntax of encapsulation is present.
A setter that accepts any value provides the same freedom as a public attribute.
No validation or rule is enforced, so invalid states are still reachable.
Genuine encapsulation means exposing operations that make sense for the object, not exposing every field.

practice.q: Explain how encapsulation makes a program easier to change, referring to the idea of an interface.
points: The public methods form the interface, which is what other code depends on.
Anything private is not depended upon and may be altered freely.
The internal storage could be replaced entirely while the interface stays the same.
Callers therefore continue to work without modification, so the change is contained within the class.

practice.q: A team is designing a Student class. Discuss how they should decide which members are public and which are private.
points: Start by identifying the operations other code genuinely needs to perform on a student.
Those operations become the public interface, expressed in terms of the problem rather than the storage.
Data that has rules attached, such as a mark that must lie between 0 and 100, should be private with validated access.
Anything only needed internally, such as a cached calculation, should be private so it can later be changed or removed.
The default should be private, because making something public later is easy but withdrawing it is not.

pages.title: Inheritance and polymorphism
pages.lede: Reusing a class by extending it, replacing one behaviour without touching the rest, and the reason a list of different things can be treated as one.

cards.a: Defining a class in terms of an existing one, so it gains that class's attributes and methods and adds or replaces what it needs.

cards.q: What are the two classes in an inheritance relationship called?
cards.a: The **superclass**, base or parent, and the **subclass**, derived or child.

cards.q: What relationship must hold for inheritance to be appropriate?
cards.a: **is-a**. A Dog is an Animal. If the sentence is false, inheritance is the wrong tool.
A subclass providing its own version of a method the superclass already defines. Calls on that subclass run the new version.
Objects of different classes responding to the same call in their own way, so one piece of code works with all of them.
The decision about which behaviour to run is made by the object's own type, not by a branch listing every case.
A class that cannot be instantiated, existing to define a common interface and shared behaviour for its subclasses.
A method declared without an implementation, which every concrete subclass must provide.

cards.q: What is composition, and how does it differ from inheritance?
cards.a: Building a class from objects of other classes — **has-a** rather than **is-a**. It is more flexible, because the parts can be swapped at run time.
Behaviour is scattered across many levels, so understanding one method means reading the whole chain, and a change high up affects everything below.

cards.q: What does it mean to call the superclass version of a method?
cards.a: Running the parent's implementation from inside the override, usually to extend it rather than replace it. In Python this is `super()`.

cards.q: What is the Liskov substitution principle, informally?
cards.a: Anywhere the superclass works, a subclass must work too. If a subclass breaks a promise the superclass made, the inheritance is wrong.

practice.q: Explain what inheritance is and state two benefits of using it.
points: A subclass is defined in terms of an existing superclass and automatically has its attributes and methods.
Shared code is written once in the superclass rather than repeated in each subclass.
A change to the shared behaviour is made in one place and applies everywhere.
Subclasses can be treated as instances of the superclass, so common code can process them together.

practice.q: Explain what method overriding is and why a subclass might do it.
points: Overriding means a subclass defines a method with the same name as one in its superclass.
Calls on objects of the subclass use the subclass's version.
It allows a subclass to specialise behaviour that differs from the general case while inheriting everything else.

practice.q: Explain what polymorphism is, using an example, and state why it reduces the need for conditional statements.
points: Polymorphism means objects of different classes respond to the same method call in their own way.
A valid example is given, such as calling `speak()` on a list containing dogs and cats.
The correct version is selected by the type of the object at run time.
The calling code therefore needs no branch listing each possible type, and requires no change when a new type is added.

practice.q: Distinguish between inheritance and composition, and state when each is appropriate.
points: Inheritance models an is-a relationship, where the subclass is a kind of the superclass.
Composition models a has-a relationship, where an object holds other objects as parts.
Inheritance is appropriate when subclasses genuinely satisfy everything promised by the superclass.
Composition is appropriate when behaviour is being reused without such a relationship, and it allows the part to be replaced at run time.

practice.q: Explain what an abstract class is and why one might be used.
points: An abstract class cannot itself be instantiated.
It defines methods that subclasses must implement, and may provide shared implementations of others.
It guarantees that every subclass offers a common interface, so they can be used interchangeably.
It prevents the creation of an object of a general type that has no meaningful concrete behaviour.

practice.q: A developer creates a class Square that inherits from Rectangle and overrides the setters so that width and height are always equal. Discuss whether this is a sound use of inheritance.
points: Mathematically a square is a rectangle, so the is-a test appears to be satisfied.
Code written for a rectangle may assume that setting the width leaves the height unchanged.
A Square breaks that assumption, so it cannot safely be used everywhere a Rectangle can.
This violates the principle that a subclass must be substitutable for its superclass.
A reasoned alternative is given, such as making both immutable, or using a common Shape interface rather than inheriting.

practice.q: Explain why a deep inheritance hierarchy can make a program harder to maintain.
points: Behaviour of one object is defined across several classes, so understanding it means reading the whole chain.
It is not obvious from a subclass which version of a method will actually run.
A change to a class high in the hierarchy affects every class beneath it, possibly unintentionally.
Subclasses become tightly coupled to their parents' implementations, so those cannot be changed freely.

pages.title: Designing with objects
pages.lede: Turning a written problem into classes, reading a UML diagram, and knowing which relationship line to draw between two boxes.

cards.q: What is a UML class diagram?
cards.a: A standard drawing of the classes in a system: a box per class with its attributes and methods, and lines showing how the classes relate.

cards.q: What are the three compartments of a UML class box?
cards.a: The class name, the attributes, and the methods.

cards.q: What do `+` and `−` mean in a UML class box?
cards.a: `+` marks a public member, `−` a private one, and `#` a protected one.
A plain line: one class knows about another and can use it, with no ownership implied.

cards.q: What is aggregation, and how is it drawn?
cards.a: A has-a relationship where the parts can exist without the whole. An open diamond at the whole's end.

cards.q: What is composition, and how is it drawn?
cards.a: A stronger has-a where the parts are owned and die with the whole. A filled diamond at the whole's end.
A line with a hollow triangle pointing at the superclass.
The numbers on the ends of a relationship saying how many objects take part — `1`, `0..1`, `1..*` or `*`.

cards.q: What is a useful first step in identifying classes from a problem description?
cards.a: Underline the nouns as candidate classes and the verbs as candidate methods, then discard the ones that are not worth modelling.

cards.q: What is meant by a class having a single responsibility?
cards.a: It does one job, so there is only one kind of change that would require it to be rewritten.
How much one class depends on the internals of another. Loose coupling means a class can be changed without disturbing its neighbours.
How closely the parts of a class belong together. High cohesion means everything in the class serves its one job.

practice.q: Describe the information shown in a UML class diagram.
points: Each class is drawn as a box divided into name, attributes and methods.
Visibility is shown by symbols such as + for public and − for private.
Lines between boxes show relationships such as association, aggregation, composition and inheritance.
Multiplicities on the line ends show how many objects participate in each relationship.

practice.q: Explain the difference between aggregation and composition, giving an example of each.
points: Both are has-a relationships in which one class holds objects of another.
In aggregation the parts can exist independently of the whole.
In composition the parts belong to the whole and are destroyed with it.
Valid examples are given, such as a team aggregating players, and a book composed of pages.

practice.q: A school library system must let members borrow and return books, and produce a list of overdue loans. Identify four suitable classes and justify one of them.
points: Sensible classes are identified, such as Member, Book, Loan and Library.
Each corresponds to a distinct thing in the problem with its own data.
A justification is given, for example that a Loan has its own attributes such as the date due, so it cannot simply be a field of Book.
The operations of the system map onto methods of these classes.

practice.q: Explain what is meant by high cohesion and why it is desirable.
points: A class has high cohesion when everything in it contributes to a single, clearly stated responsibility.
Such a class is easier to name, understand and test.
Only one kind of requirement change forces it to be rewritten, so changes stay contained.

practice.q: Explain what is meant by coupling, and describe how it can be reduced between two classes.
points: Coupling is the degree to which one class depends on another.
Tight coupling occurs when one class relies on another's internal data or implementation.
Reducing coupling means depending only on a small public interface.
The other class can then be changed or replaced without altering the first.

practice.q: A student designs a single class, GameManager, that holds the board, the players, the scores, the rules and the display code. Discuss the problems with this design and how it should be improved.
points: The class has many unrelated responsibilities, so it has low cohesion.
Any change to the display, the rules or the scoring requires editing the same class, increasing the risk of breaking unrelated behaviour.
It cannot be tested in parts, because the game logic cannot be exercised without the display.
It should be split into classes such as Board, Player, Rules and Display, each with one responsibility.
The manager then coordinates those objects, depending only on their public interfaces.

practice.q: Explain how identifying nouns and verbs in a problem statement helps in designing classes, and state one limitation of the technique.
points: Nouns suggest candidate classes or attributes, since they name things in the problem domain.
Verbs suggest candidate methods, since they name things that can be done.
It provides a systematic starting point rather than requiring the design to be invented from nothing.
A limitation is that it over-produces, since many nouns are attributes or irrelevant, so the list must be filtered by judgement.

pages.title: Abstract data types
pages.lede: The difference between what a structure promises and how it is built, and why an array and a linked list are good at opposite things.

cards.q: What is an abstract data type?
cards.a: A description of the values a structure holds and the operations it supports, with nothing said about how it is stored.

cards.q: What is the difference between an ADT and a data structure?
cards.a: The ADT is the promise — push, pop, isEmpty. The data structure is the implementation that keeps it, such as an array or linked nodes.

cards.q: Why is separating the two useful?
cards.a: Code written against the operations keeps working when the storage is replaced, so the implementation can be changed for performance without rewriting callers.

cards.q: What is a static data structure?
cards.a: One whose size is fixed when it is created, such as an array. Memory is allocated once and cannot grow.

cards.q: What is a dynamic data structure?
cards.a: One that grows and shrinks while the program runs, allocating memory for each element as it is needed.

cards.q: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of a static structure.
cards.a: Access by index is immediate because the address can be calculated. But the size must be guessed in advance, wasting memory or running out.

cards.q: Why can an array be indexed in constant time?
cards.a: Elements are the same size and stored consecutively, so the address is $\text{base} + \text{index} \times \text{size}$ — one calculation regardless of length.

cards.q: What does it cost to insert at the front of an array?
cards.a: Every existing element must be shifted up one place, so the work is proportional to the length of the array.

cards.q: What is a record, or struct?
cards.a: A group of named fields of possibly different types, treated as one value. It is the building block for the node of a dynamic structure.

cards.q: What is a pointer or reference?
cards.a: A value holding the address of something else. It is what allows a node to link to another node held anywhere in memory.

cards.q: Name four common abstract data types.
cards.a: Stack, queue, list, and tree. A set, a map and a graph are also ADTs.

cards.q: How do you choose a data structure?
cards.a: By which operations the program performs most: indexing, inserting in the middle, searching, or taking from the ends.

practice.q: Explain what is meant by an abstract data type, and distinguish it from a data structure.
points: An ADT specifies the data it holds and the operations that may be performed on it.
It says nothing about how the data is physically stored.
A data structure is a concrete implementation, such as an array or a set of linked nodes.
The same ADT can therefore be implemented by more than one data structure.

practice.q: Explain why separating an ADT from its implementation is useful when a program must be maintained.
points: Code that uses the ADT depends only on its operations.
The implementation can be replaced without changing any calling code.
A structure can therefore be swapped for a faster one if performance becomes a problem.
Faults in the implementation are confined to one place rather than spread through the program.

practice.q: Compare static and dynamic data structures.
points: A static structure has a size fixed when it is created; a dynamic one grows and shrinks at run time.
A static structure allocates one block of memory, allowing an element's address to be calculated directly.
A dynamic structure allocates memory per element, so it uses only what is needed but stores a pointer with each element.
A static structure may waste memory or overflow if the size is guessed wrongly, which a dynamic one avoids.

practice.q: Explain why an element of an array can be accessed in constant time.
points: Every element occupies the same number of bytes.
Elements are stored consecutively, so the address is the base address plus the index times the element size.
The calculation takes the same time regardless of the index or the length of the array.

practice.q: A program repeatedly inserts new values at the front of a collection of 10,000 items. Explain why an array performs poorly and what should be used instead.
points: Inserting at the front of an array requires every existing element to be moved up one position.
Each insertion therefore costs work proportional to the number of items, around 10,000 moves.
A linked list inserts at the front by creating a node and changing one pointer.
This takes the same short time regardless of how many items are already stored.

practice.q: Explain what a pointer is and why dynamic data structures depend on them.
points: A pointer holds the memory address of another item of data.
Nodes in a dynamic structure are allocated separately and are not adjacent in memory.
Each node therefore stores a pointer to the next, which is what connects them into a structure.
Following pointers is how the structure is traversed, and rearranging them is how it is modified.

practice.q: A team must store a school's 1,200 student records. Discuss which data structure they should choose, given that records are looked up by ID far more often than they are added or removed.
points: The dominant operation is lookup by a key, not insertion or traversal in order.
Searching a list or array of 1,200 records examines up to 1,200 entries per lookup.
A hash table or dictionary keyed by student ID finds a record in roughly constant time.
A sorted array with binary search is an alternative, costing about eleven comparisons, but insertions then require shifting.
A justified conclusion is reached, noting the extra memory a hash table uses is a reasonable price given the access pattern.

pages.title: Stacks and queues
pages.lede: Two structures defined by what they refuse to let you do, and the reason both turn up everywhere from undo buttons to printers.

cards.a: A collection where items are added and removed at the same end. **Last in, first out**.
`push` adds to the top, `pop` removes and returns the top, `peek` or `top` looks without removing, and `isEmpty` reports whether anything is there.
A collection where items are added at the rear and removed from the front. **First in, first out**.
`enqueue` adds at the rear, `dequeue` removes and returns the front, `peek` looks at the front, and `isEmpty` reports whether anything is there.
Pushing onto a stack that has no room left. In a program it usually means uncontrolled recursion.
Popping from an empty stack. The operation must be refused rather than returning nonsense.

cards.q: Give three uses of a stack.
cards.a: The call stack for function calls, undo history, and evaluating expressions or matching brackets.

cards.q: Give three uses of a queue.
cards.a: A print spooler, keystrokes waiting to be processed, and packets buffered at a router.

cards.q: What is a circular queue and why is it used?
cards.a: A fixed array in which the front and rear indices wrap round with modulo. It reuses freed space without shifting elements down.

cards.q: Why not implement a queue as an array with the front always at index 0?
cards.a: Every dequeue would shift all remaining elements one place, making removal cost work proportional to the length.
A queue where each item has a priority and the highest-priority item leaves first, regardless of arrival order.

cards.q: How do you tell a full circular queue from an empty one?
cards.a: Both give `front == rear`, so either keep a count of items or leave one slot always unused.

practice.q: Describe the operations of a stack and state the order in which items are removed.
points: push adds an item to the top of the stack.
pop removes and returns the item at the top.
peek returns the top item without removing it, and isEmpty tests whether the stack holds anything.
Items are removed in the reverse of the order they were added, which is last in, first out.

practice.q: Explain the difference between a stack and a queue, giving one appropriate use of each.
points: A stack adds and removes at the same end, so the most recently added item leaves first.
A queue adds at one end and removes from the other, so the earliest item leaves first.
A suitable stack application is given, such as undo or the call stack.
A suitable queue application is given, such as a print spooler or a network buffer.

practice.q: The values 4, 9, 2 and 7 are pushed onto a stack in that order, then two items are popped and 5 is pushed. State the contents of the stack from top to bottom and explain your answer.
points: After the four pushes the stack from top to bottom is 7, 2, 9, 4.
The two pops remove 7 and then 2, because the most recent item leaves first.
Pushing 5 places it on top of the remaining items.
The final contents from top to bottom are 5, 9, 4.

practice.q: Explain why a circular queue is used in preference to a simple array-based queue.
points: In a simple array queue, removing from the front either shifts every remaining element or leaves the space unusable.
Shifting makes each dequeue cost work proportional to the number of items.
A circular queue advances the front index instead, using modulo arithmetic so it wraps to the start.
Space freed at the front is therefore reused, and both operations take constant time.

practice.q: Explain what stack overflow and stack underflow are, and how a well-written implementation should respond to each.
points: Overflow occurs when a push is attempted on a stack with no remaining capacity.
Underflow occurs when a pop or peek is attempted on an empty stack.
Each must be detected and reported rather than allowed to read or write invalid memory.
The operation should be refused, for example by raising an error, so the calling code can handle it.

practice.q: Describe how a stack is used to check that the brackets in an expression are correctly matched.
points: Each character of the expression is examined in turn.
An opening bracket is pushed onto the stack.
On a closing bracket, the stack is popped and the popped bracket must be of the matching type.
If the stack is empty when a closing bracket is met, or the types do not match, the expression is invalid.
The expression is valid only if the stack is empty once every character has been examined.

practice.q: A hospital wishes to treat patients in arrival order, except that emergencies are seen first. Explain which abstract data type is appropriate and why a simple queue is not.
points: A simple queue always removes the earliest arrival, so an emergency would wait behind routine cases.
A priority queue is appropriate, in which each patient is given a priority.
The item with the highest priority is removed first, regardless of when it was added.
Patients of equal priority are still served in arrival order, so fairness within a priority level is preserved.

pages.title: Linked lists
pages.lede: A collection held together by pointers rather than by position, the four operations you must be able to trace, and the order in which to rewire them.

cards.a: A dynamic structure of nodes, each holding a value and a pointer to the next node. The list is reached through a pointer to the first node.
A record holding the data and one or more pointers. In a singly linked list it holds the value and `next`.
The pointer to the first node. Lose the head and the whole list is unreachable.

cards.q: How is the end of a list marked?
cards.a: The last node's `next` pointer is null, which is what a traversal tests for.

cards.q: How do you traverse a linked list?
cards.a: Start at the head, use the value, follow `next`, and stop when the pointer is null.

cards.q: What is the cost of inserting at the front?
cards.a: Constant. Create the node, point it at the current head, then make the head point at it.

cards.q: Why must the order of pointer assignments be right when inserting?
cards.a: Overwriting a pointer before copying it loses the rest of the list, which then cannot be recovered.
The previous node's `next` is set to the deleted node's `next`, so the list skips it. Deleting the head means moving the head pointer.

cards.q: What is a doubly linked list?
cards.a: Each node holds a pointer to the next **and** the previous node, allowing traversal in both directions at the cost of another pointer per node.

cards.q: What is a circular linked list?
cards.a: One where the last node points back to the first rather than to null, so traversal can continue indefinitely.

cards.q: Give two advantages of a linked list over an array.
cards.a: It grows and shrinks as needed with no fixed limit, and insertion or deletion at a known position takes constant time with no shifting.

cards.q: Give two disadvantages of a linked list.
cards.a: There is no direct access by index, so reaching the $n$th node takes $n$ steps, and every node costs extra memory for its pointer.

practice.q: Describe the structure of a singly linked list.
points: It consists of nodes, each holding a data value and a pointer.
Each node's pointer holds the address of the next node.
A head pointer identifies the first node in the list.
The final node's pointer is null, marking the end.

practice.q: Describe an algorithm to insert a new node at the front of a linked list.
points: Create the new node and store the value in it.
Set the new node's next pointer to the current head.
Set the head pointer to the new node.
The operation takes constant time as no existing nodes are moved.

practice.q: Explain why the order of the pointer assignments matters when inserting a node into a linked list.
points: Each node is reachable only through the pointer that refers to it.
If the previous node's pointer is overwritten first, the address of the rest of the list is lost.
Nothing then refers to those nodes, so they cannot be recovered.
The existing pointer must therefore be copied into the new node before it is overwritten.

practice.q: Describe how a node holding a given value is deleted from a singly linked list.
points: Traverse the list keeping a reference to the previous node as well as the current one.
Stop when the current node holds the value being sought, or the end is reached.
Set the previous node's next pointer to the current node's next pointer, so the list bypasses it.
If the node to delete is the head, move the head pointer to the second node instead.

practice.q: Compare a singly linked list with a doubly linked list.
points: A singly linked node stores one pointer, to the next node; a doubly linked node also stores one to the previous node.
A doubly linked list can be traversed in both directions.
Deleting a known node is simpler, as the previous node can be reached without traversing from the head.
The cost is extra memory per node and two pointers to maintain correctly on every change.

practice.q: A program must store a queue of tasks that is frequently added to and removed from, and whose maximum length is unknown. Explain why a linked list is a better choice than an array.
points: The maximum length is unknown, so an array's size would have to be guessed.
Too small an array overflows and too large a one wastes memory, while a linked list allocates only what is used.
Additions and removals at the ends take constant time in a linked list with head and tail pointers.
An array-based queue would require shifting elements or the extra complexity of circular indices.

practice.q: Explain how a linked list is traversed, and discuss why searching one cannot use binary search.
points: Traversal begins at the head and follows each node's next pointer in turn.
Each node's value is examined until the target is found or a null pointer is reached.
Binary search requires jumping directly to the middle element of the range being searched.
A linked list provides no way to calculate the address of the middle node, as nodes are not stored consecutively.
Reaching the middle would itself require traversing half the list, so the halving would give no saving.

pages.title: Trees and binary search trees
pages.lede: A structure with more than one next, the one rule that makes searching fast, and the three traversals you have to be able to write out.

cards.a: A structure of nodes in which each node has one parent and any number of children, with a single root and no cycles.

cards.q: Define root, leaf, parent and child.
cards.a: The **root** is the only node with no parent. A **leaf** has no children. A **parent** points to its **children**, which are the nodes directly below it.

cards.q: What is the height of a tree?
cards.a: The number of levels. Counting edges instead of levels gives a number one smaller, so say which you mean.
A tree in which every node has at most two children, called the left and right child.

cards.q: What rule defines a binary search tree?
cards.a: For every node, all values in its left subtree are smaller and all values in its right subtree are larger.

cards.q: How is a value searched for in a binary search tree?
cards.a: Compare with the current node; go left if smaller, right if larger, stop when equal or when the pointer is null.

cards.q: What is the cost of searching a balanced binary search tree?
cards.a: $O(\log n)$, because each comparison discards one of the two subtrees.

cards.q: What happens if values are inserted into a binary search tree in sorted order?
cards.a: Every node has only a right child, so the tree degenerates into a linked list and searching becomes $O(n)$.

cards.q: What is an in-order traversal, and what is it used for?
cards.a: Left subtree, node, right subtree. On a binary search tree it visits the values in ascending order.

cards.q: What is a pre-order traversal used for?
cards.a: Node, left, right. It outputs a tree in an order that rebuilds the same shape, so it is used for copying and serialising.

cards.q: What is a post-order traversal used for?
cards.a: Left, right, node. Children are always finished before the parent, so it is used for deleting a tree and for evaluating expression trees.
One in which the subtrees of every node differ in height by at most a small fixed amount, keeping the height around $\log_2 n$.

practice.q: Define the terms root, leaf, subtree and height as they apply to a tree.
points: The root is the single node at the top, which has no parent.
A leaf is a node with no children.
A subtree is a node together with all of its descendants.
The height is the number of levels — equivalently, one more than the number of edges on the longest root-to-leaf path.

practice.q: State the property that defines a binary search tree and explain why it makes searching efficient.
points: For every node, all values in the left subtree are less than it and all values in the right subtree are greater.
Comparing the target with a node determines which subtree it must be in, if it is present at all.
The other subtree can therefore be discarded entirely, halving the remaining search in a balanced tree.

practice.q: The values 50, 30, 70, 20 and 40 are inserted into an empty binary search tree in that order. Describe the resulting tree and explain how 40 reached its position.
points: 50 becomes the root, with 30 as its left child and 70 as its right child.
20 is less than 50 and less than 30, so it becomes the left child of 30.
40 is less than 50 so it goes left, then greater than 30 so it goes right.
The position under 30 is empty, so 40 becomes the right child of 30.

practice.q: State the order in which nodes are visited by in-order, pre-order and post-order traversals, and give a use for each.
points: In-order visits the left subtree, the node, then the right subtree, and outputs a binary search tree in sorted order.
Pre-order visits the node, then the left subtree, then the right subtree, and can be used to copy or serialise a tree.
Post-order visits the left subtree, the right subtree, then the node, and is used to delete a tree or evaluate an expression tree.
In each case the traversal of a subtree follows the same rule recursively.

practice.q: Explain what happens if data is inserted into a binary search tree in ascending order, and state the effect on search performance.
points: Each new value is larger than every existing one, so it is placed as the right child of the previous node.
The tree becomes a single chain with no left children.
Its height equals the number of nodes rather than about log n.
Searching must follow the whole chain, so performance degrades from O(log n) to O(n).

practice.q: Compare storing 1,000,000 sorted values in a balanced binary search tree with storing them in a sorted array, considering both searching and insertion.
points: Both allow searching in about twenty comparisons, as both halve the range at each step.
Inserting into a sorted array requires shifting elements, costing up to 1,000,000 moves.
Inserting into a balanced tree requires following one path and changing a pointer, costing about twenty steps.
The array uses less memory, as the tree stores two pointers with every value.
A justified conclusion is reached, for example that the tree is preferable when the data changes and the array when it is fixed.

practice.q: Explain why an in-order traversal of a binary search tree produces the values in ascending order.
points: Every value in a node's left subtree is smaller than the node.
Every value in its right subtree is larger.
Visiting the left subtree first, then the node, then the right subtree therefore emits smaller values before larger ones.
The same holds recursively at every node, so the whole sequence is ordered.

pages.title: Recursion
pages.lede: A function that calls itself, why it needs a base case more than it needs anything else, and what it is actually building in memory while it runs.

cards.a: A function defined in terms of itself: it solves a small case directly and solves a larger one by calling itself on something smaller.

cards.q: What two parts must every recursive function have?
cards.a: A **base case** that returns without recursing, and a **recursive case** that calls itself on a strictly smaller problem.

cards.q: What happens if the base case is missing or unreachable?
cards.a: The calls never stop, the stack fills, and the program crashes with a stack overflow.
The block of memory holding one call's parameters, local variables and return address. Each active call has its own.

cards.q: Why does recursion use more memory than iteration?
cards.a: Every call that has not yet returned occupies a frame on the call stack, so depth $n$ costs $n$ frames. A loop reuses one.

cards.q: What is the recursive definition of factorial?
cards.a: $n! = 1$ when $n \le 1$, and $n! = n \times (n-1)!$ otherwise.

cards.q: Why is naive recursive Fibonacci so slow?
cards.a: It recomputes the same values repeatedly. The number of calls grows exponentially, roughly doubling for each increase of one in $n$.
Storing the result of each call so a repeated call returns the stored answer instead of recomputing it.

cards.q: When is recursion the better choice?
cards.a: When the data or the problem is itself recursive — trees, nested structures, divide and conquer — so the code matches the shape of the problem.

cards.q: When is iteration the better choice?
cards.a: When the problem is a straightforward repetition, where a loop is clearer and avoids the memory and call cost.
A recursive call that is the last thing the function does. Some languages turn it into a loop, reusing one frame instead of many.

cards.q: Why is every tree algorithm naturally recursive?
cards.a: Because every subtree is itself a tree, so the same procedure applies unchanged to a smaller input.

practice.q: Define recursion and state the two components every recursive algorithm must have.
points: Recursion is a technique in which a function calls itself to solve a smaller instance of the same problem.
A base case gives a result directly, without any further call.
A recursive case calls the function on a smaller input and combines the result.

practice.q: Explain what happens in memory when a recursive function is called several times before any call returns.
points: Each call places a new stack frame on the call stack.
The frame holds that call's parameters, local variables and return address.
Frames accumulate until the base case is reached, so no result is produced until then.
Frames are then removed in reverse order as each call returns to the one that made it.

practice.q: Trace the recursive calculation of `factorial(4)`, showing the calls and the values returned.
points: factorial(4) calls factorial(3), which calls factorial(2), which calls factorial(1).
factorial(1) meets the base case and returns 1 without recursing.
The returns then unwind: factorial(2) returns 2, factorial(3) returns 6.
factorial(4) returns 4 × 6 = 24.

practice.q: Explain why a recursive solution may fail with a stack overflow where an iterative one would not.
points: Each unreturned recursive call occupies a stack frame.
The call stack has a limited size, typically allowing a few thousand frames.
A recursion whose depth exceeds this exhausts the stack and the program terminates.
An iterative solution reuses a single frame regardless of the number of repetitions.

practice.q: The naive recursive Fibonacci function is extremely slow for moderate inputs. Explain why, and describe one way to improve it.
points: Each call makes two further calls, so the number of calls grows exponentially with n.
The same subproblems are computed many times, for example fib(3) being recalculated repeatedly.
Memoisation stores each computed result so a repeated call returns it immediately.
This reduces the work to one calculation per value, making the running time linear.

practice.q: Compare recursion and iteration as ways of solving a problem, and state when each is preferable.
points: Both can express repetition, and any recursive solution can in principle be written iteratively.
Recursion uses stack memory proportional to its depth, whereas iteration uses a fixed amount.
Recursion carries the overhead of a function call for each step, so it is generally slower.
Recursion is clearer when the data or problem is itself recursive, such as traversing a tree.
Iteration is preferable for simple repetition, where a loop is both clearer and cheaper.

practice.q: Explain why traversing a binary tree is usually written recursively rather than iteratively.
points: Each child of a node is itself the root of a subtree, so the same procedure applies to it.
The recursive code therefore states the definition of the traversal directly.
Writing it iteratively requires an explicit stack to remember which nodes still need visiting.
That stack duplicates by hand what the call stack does automatically, making the code longer and easier to get wrong.

pages.title: Searching, sorting and complexity
pages.lede: The five algorithms you must be able to trace, the notation for saying how badly they scale, and why the difference is not about speed but about shape.

cards.q: How does a linear search work?
cards.a: Examine each element in turn until the target is found or the end is reached. It needs no ordering.

cards.q: What is the cost of a linear search?
cards.a: $O(n)$. On average $n/2$ comparisons, and $n$ in the worst case.

cards.q: How does a binary search work?
cards.a: Compare with the middle element of the range; discard the half that cannot contain the target; repeat until found or the range is empty.

cards.q: What must be true before a binary search can be used?
cards.a: The data must already be sorted on the key being searched.

cards.q: What is the cost of a binary search?
cards.a: $O(\log n)$ — at most $\lceil \log_2 n \rceil$ comparisons, so about 20 for a million items.

cards.q: How does a bubble sort work?
cards.a: Repeatedly pass through the list swapping adjacent elements that are out of order, until a pass makes no swaps.

cards.q: How does a selection sort work?
cards.a: Find the smallest remaining element and swap it into the next position, repeating for each position in turn.

cards.q: How does an insertion sort work?
cards.a: Take each element in turn and slide it back into its correct place among the elements already sorted.

cards.q: Which simple sort is best on nearly sorted data, and why?
cards.a: Insertion sort. Each element moves only a short distance, so it approaches $O(n)$ rather than $O(n^2)$.
Split the list in half repeatedly until each part holds one element, then merge pairs back together in order.
There are $\log_2 n$ levels of merging, and each level does $n$ work merging every element once.
How the work grows with the size of the input, ignoring constant factors and lower-order terms.
One that keeps equal elements in their original relative order, which matters when sorting by one key after another.

practice.q: Compare linear search and binary search, stating the conditions under which each can be used.
points: Linear search examines each element in turn and works on data in any order.
Binary search repeatedly halves the range and requires the data to be sorted.
Linear search takes O(n) comparisons while binary search takes O(log n).
Linear search is preferable for small or unsorted data, since sorting first may cost more than it saves.

practice.q: A sorted array holds 1,000,000 records. State the maximum number of comparisons needed by a binary search and explain your answer.
points: Each comparison discards half of the remaining elements.
The number of comparisons is therefore the number of times 1,000,000 can be halved.
This is log₂ 1,000,000, which is approximately 20.
At most 20 comparisons are needed, compared with up to 1,000,000 for a linear search.

practice.q: Describe how a bubble sort orders a list, and explain how the algorithm can detect that it has finished early.
points: Adjacent pairs of elements are compared and swapped if they are in the wrong order.
Each complete pass moves the largest remaining element to its final position at the end.
A flag records whether any swap occurred during a pass.
If a pass completes with no swaps the list is already sorted, so the algorithm stops.

practice.q: Explain why merge sort is O(n log n) while bubble sort is O(n²).
points: Merge sort divides the list in half repeatedly, giving log₂ n levels.
Each level merges every element exactly once, so each level costs n operations.
Bubble sort makes a pass for each element, and each pass compares up to n elements.
Its work is therefore proportional to n × n rather than n × log n.

practice.q: Explain what big-O notation describes and why constant factors are ignored.
points: Big-O describes how the running time or memory grows as the input size increases.
It classifies algorithms by the shape of that growth rather than by exact timings.
Constant factors depend on the machine and language, so they do not distinguish algorithms.
For large inputs the fastest-growing term dominates, so lower-order terms and constants become insignificant.

practice.q: A program must sort 20 items once, and another must sort 2,000,000 items repeatedly. Discuss which sorting algorithm each should use.
points: For 20 items the difference in growth is irrelevant, since both finish almost instantly.
Insertion sort is a reasonable choice there, being simple to write and fast on small or nearly sorted data.
For 2,000,000 items an O(n²) sort would require around four trillion operations and is not viable.
Merge sort or a comparable O(n log n) algorithm requires around forty million, which is practical.
A justified conclusion is reached, noting that merge sort's extra memory requirement is an acceptable cost at that size.

practice.q: Explain what is meant by a stable sort and give a situation in which stability matters.
points: A stable sort preserves the original relative order of elements that compare as equal.
An unstable sort may reorder such elements arbitrarily.
It matters when data is sorted by one key and then by another.
For example, sorting by name and then by class keeps each class's names in alphabetical order only if the second sort is stable.

pages.title: What a computer actually is
pages.lede: Before any of the detail, the one idea the whole subject rests on — a machine that stores its own instructions and follows them without understanding them.

cards.a: A machine that holds both its **data and its instructions** in the same memory, and works through those instructions one at a time. Changing what it does means changing the contents of memory, not the wiring.

cards.q: Why does it matter that instructions live in the same memory as data?
cards.a: Because a program becomes something the machine can *store, copy and change* like any other data. It is what makes a computer general-purpose rather than a fixed appliance.

cards.q: What are the four things every computer does?
cards.a: **Input**, **processing**, **storage**, **output**. Everything else in the course is detail hanging off one of those four.

cards.q: Does a computer understand the instructions it follows?
cards.a: No. Each instruction is a pattern of bits that causes a fixed electrical effect. Meaning exists only in the mind of the programmer.

cards.q: What is the difference between hardware and software?
cards.a: Hardware is the physical machinery; software is the pattern of bits in memory that tells it what to do. The same hardware runs any software you load into it.
One of two distinguishable states, written $0$ and $1$. Physically it is a voltage that is either low or high — never anything in between, by design.

cards.q: Why do computers use two states rather than ten?
cards.a: Because telling *low* from *high* survives noise, heat and manufacturing variation. Distinguishing ten voltage levels reliably, billions of times a second, does not.
One machine that can be made to do any computable task by loading a different program, rather than being built for one job.

cards.q: In one sentence, what is an algorithm?
cards.a: A finite sequence of unambiguous steps that turns an input into the intended output.

cards.q: Why is a pocket calculator not a general-purpose computer?
cards.a: Its behaviour is fixed by its wiring. You cannot load a new program into it and make it do something its designers did not build in.

practice.q: State what is meant by a **stored-program computer**.
points: Instructions are held in memory alongside the data / in the same memory as data.
The processor fetches and executes those instructions one at a time / in sequence.

practice.q: Explain why storing instructions in memory makes a computer general-purpose.
points: A program is just data in memory, so it can be loaded, replaced or changed.
Changing the task therefore requires no change to the hardware / no rewiring.
One machine can therefore perform any task for which a program can be written.

practice.q: A student says "the computer understands my Python program". Explain why this is not accurate, referring to what the processor actually does.
points: The processor only ever acts on patterns of bits / binary instructions.
Each instruction causes a fixed electrical effect in the hardware, with no meaning attached.
Python must first be translated into those instructions before anything can run.
Meaning is supplied by the programmer, not the machine / the machine has no model of the problem.

practice.q: Identify the four stages of the general computing model and give an example of each in a supermarket self-checkout.
points: Input — scanning a barcode / touching the screen / inserting a card.
Processing — looking up the price, adding to the total, checking the payment.
Output — the display, the receipt, the printed label (storage also credited if described).

practice.q: Explain why digital computers represent information using two states rather than ten.
points: Two states can be represented by a voltage being clearly low or clearly high.
This tolerates noise, temperature change and manufacturing variation, because a small drift does not change which state is read.
Ten levels would need the circuit to distinguish much smaller differences reliably.
Errors would therefore be far more frequent at the speeds and scales involved.

practice.q: Distinguish between hardware and software, and explain why the distinction is less sharp than it first appears.
points: Hardware is the physical machinery; software is the instructions and data held in memory.
The same hardware performs completely different tasks depending on the software loaded.
The boundary blurs — firmware, and hardware that is itself configurable — so the distinction is about role rather than substance.

practice.q: A washing machine contains a processor, memory and a program. Discuss whether it should be called a computer.
points: It does contain the components of a computer — processor, memory, stored instructions.
It performs input, processing and output, so it fits the general model.
However its program is fixed and cannot be replaced by the user, so it is an embedded system.
It is therefore a computer in construction but special-purpose in use.
A defensible conclusion is stated either way, supported by the points above.

pages.title: Inside the processor
pages.lede: The four parts every CPU has, what each one is physically for, and why the design has barely changed in eighty years.

cards.q: What are the main components of a CPU?
cards.a: The **control unit**, the **arithmetic and logic unit**, a set of **registers**, and the **buses** connecting them to memory.

cards.q: What does the control unit do?
cards.a: It decodes each instruction and sends the timing and control signals that make the rest of the hardware carry it out. It computes nothing itself — it is the conductor, not a player.
Arithmetic ($+$, $-$, and often $\times$) and logic (AND, OR, NOT, comparisons, shifts). It is where the actual work happens.
A very small, very fast store inside the CPU itself — typically 32 or 64 bits. Reaching one costs a fraction of a nanosecond, against tens of nanoseconds for main memory.

cards.q: What does the program counter (PC) hold?
cards.a: The **address of the next instruction** to fetch. Not the instruction — the address of it.

cards.q: What does the memory address register (MAR) hold?
cards.a: The address currently being read from or written to. It is what drives the address bus.

cards.q: What does the memory data register (MDR) hold?
cards.a: The data just read from memory, or about to be written to it. Everything travelling between the CPU and memory passes through it.
The result of the ALU's most recent operation, ready to be used by the next one or written back to memory.

cards.q: What is the current instruction register (CIR)?
cards.a: The register holding the instruction currently being decoded and executed.

cards.q: What are the three buses and what does each carry?
cards.a: **Address bus** — which location (one way, CPU to memory). **Data bus** — the value itself (two way). **Control bus** — signals such as read, write and clock (mixed).

cards.q: Why is the address bus one-directional but the data bus two-directional?
cards.a: Only the CPU ever says which address it wants, so addresses travel one way. Data travels out on a write and in on a read, so it needs both.

cards.q: How does the width of the address bus limit a computer?
cards.a: $n$ address lines can name $2^n$ locations. A 32-bit address bus can therefore reach only $2^{32}$ bytes, which is 4 GiB — the historical reason for the move to 64-bit.

practice.q: Describe the role of the control unit and the arithmetic and logic unit, making clear how they differ.
points: The control unit decodes instructions and issues control signals to the other components.
It sequences and coordinates operations, including timing, but performs no calculation itself.
The ALU performs arithmetic operations such as addition and subtraction.
The ALU also performs logical operations and comparisons, producing the results and status flags.

practice.q: Explain why registers are used at all, given that the computer already has main memory.
points: Registers are inside the CPU, so access takes a fraction of the time main memory does.
Instructions need somewhere to hold operands and intermediate results while executing.
Using main memory for this would leave the CPU waiting on every step, wasting most of its speed.

practice.q: State the purpose of the program counter, the memory address register, the memory data register and the current instruction register.
points: PC — holds the address of the next instruction to be fetched.
MAR — holds the address of the memory location currently being accessed.
MDR — holds the data being transferred to or from memory.
CIR — holds the instruction currently being decoded and executed.

practice.q: A processor has a 16-bit address bus and an 8-bit data bus. Calculate the maximum memory it can address, and state the units.
points: $2^{16} = 65{,}536$ addressable locations.
Each location holds 8 bits, that is one byte, because the data bus is 8 bits wide.
Maximum addressable memory is therefore $65{,}536$ bytes, that is 64 KiB.

practice.q: Explain why the address bus is unidirectional while the data bus is bidirectional.
points: The CPU is always the component that specifies which address is wanted.
Memory never sends an address back, so a return path would be unused.
Data must travel from memory to the CPU when reading.
Data must travel from the CPU to memory when writing, so both directions are needed.

practice.q: Explain what the control bus is for, giving two examples of signals it carries.
points: It carries the signals that coordinate and time the actions of the components.
Example — a read or write signal telling memory which operation is wanted.
Example — the clock signal, or an interrupt request, which synchronises or redirects activity.

practice.q: A manufacturer widens a processor's data bus from 32 bits to 64 bits, leaving the clock speed unchanged. Discuss the effect on performance.
points: Twice as much data moves between CPU and memory per transfer.
Programs handling large values or large blocks of data need fewer transfers, so they run faster.
Programs limited by something else — dependent calculations, or waiting on input — see little or no gain.
The wider bus costs more in pins, tracks and power, so the benefit is not free.
A supported conclusion is reached, for example that the benefit depends on whether the workload is memory-bound.

pages.title: The fetch–decode–execute cycle
pages.lede: The loop the processor has been running since you turned the machine on, traced register by register until there is nothing mysterious left in it.

cards.q: What are the three stages of the machine cycle?
cards.a: **Fetch** the next instruction from memory, **decode** it to work out what it means, **execute** it. Then repeat, forever.

cards.q: Write out the fetch stage as register transfers.
cards.a: $\text{MAR} \leftarrow \text{PC}$; then memory is read so $\text{MDR} \leftarrow [\text{MAR}]$; then $\text{CIR} \leftarrow \text{MDR}$; and $\text{PC} \leftarrow \text{PC} + 1$.

cards.q: When is the program counter incremented, and why then?
cards.a: During the **fetch** stage, right after the address has been used. Doing it early means a jump instruction executed later can simply overwrite the PC, without the increment undoing it.
The control unit splits the instruction in the CIR into its **opcode** (what to do) and its **operand** (what to do it to), and works out which control signals the operation needs.
The part of an instruction saying which operation is wanted — load, store, add, jump. Typically the first few bits.
The part of an instruction saying what to operate on: a value, a register, or more often the address of one.

cards.q: How does a jump instruction work, mechanically?
cards.a: Execute writes the jump's operand into the **program counter**. The next fetch therefore starts somewhere else. That is the whole mechanism behind every loop, `if` and function call.

cards.q: What is the clock speed of a processor?
cards.a: How many cycles it performs per second, measured in hertz. $3\,\text{GHz}$ is $3\times10^{9}$ cycles a second.

cards.q: Does one clock cycle equal one instruction?
cards.a: No. Simple designs take several cycles per instruction; pipelined ones complete more than one per cycle on a good run. Clock speed alone does not tell you how fast a processor is.
Overlapping the stages, so one instruction is being executed while the next is decoded and a third is fetched — like a production line rather than one worker doing every step.

cards.q: Why can a branch hurt a pipeline?
cards.a: The instructions already fetched behind a jump turn out to be the wrong ones and must be discarded, leaving the pipeline to refill.

practice.q: Describe the fetch stage of the machine cycle, referring to the registers involved.
points: The address in the program counter is copied into the memory address register.
The instruction at that address is read from memory into the memory data register.
The instruction is copied from the MDR into the current instruction register.
The program counter is incremented so it points at the following instruction.

practice.q: Explain why the program counter is incremented during fetch rather than at the end of the cycle.
points: The address it held has already been used, so it is free to update.
If the instruction turns out to be a jump, execute can overwrite the PC and the increment will not interfere with it.

practice.q: Explain what happens during the decode stage.
points: The instruction held in the CIR is split into opcode and operand.
The control unit interprets the opcode to determine which operation is required.
It then generates the control signals needed by the ALU, registers and memory for that operation.

practice.q: A program contains a loop. Explain, in terms of the machine cycle, how the processor repeats instructions.
points: At the end of the loop body there is a jump or branch instruction.
During its execute stage, the operand is written into the program counter.
The next fetch therefore takes its address from the start of the loop rather than the following line.
The cycle continues as normal from there, so the same instructions are fetched again.

practice.q: Two processors are advertised at 2.5 GHz and 3.5 GHz. Explain why the second is not necessarily 40% faster.
points: Clock speed only counts cycles, not work completed per cycle.
Processors differ in how many cycles each instruction takes, and in how effectively they pipeline.
Cache size and memory speed may leave either processor waiting, whatever its clock.
The number of cores, and whether the software can use them, may matter more than clock speed.

practice.q: Explain what pipelining is and why a conditional branch reduces its benefit.
points: Pipelining overlaps the stages of consecutive instructions rather than completing one before starting the next.
While one instruction executes, the next is decoded and a third is fetched.
Throughput therefore rises, approaching one completed instruction per cycle.
At a conditional branch the processor does not yet know which instructions follow, so it may fetch the wrong ones.
Those partially processed instructions must be discarded and the pipeline refilled, costing the cycles that had been saved.

practice.q: State what is held in the MAR, the MDR and the CIR immediately after the fetch stage of an instruction stored at address 40.
points: MAR holds 40, the address that was just accessed.
MDR holds the instruction that was read from address 40.
CIR holds that same instruction, copied there ready for decoding.

pages.title: Primary memory and the hierarchy
pages.lede: Why a computer has five kinds of memory instead of one good one, and why the answer is economics rather than engineering.

cards.a: Memory the processor can address directly — RAM and ROM. Anything the CPU works on must be here first.
The contents are lost when power is removed. RAM is volatile; ROM and secondary storage are not.
Holding the programs currently running and the data they are working on. It is read/write and volatile.
Holding the instructions needed to start the machine — the bootstrap or firmware. Non-volatile, so something is there before anything has been loaded.

cards.q: Why does a computer need ROM as well as RAM?
cards.a: At power-on RAM is empty and there is no operating system yet. Something non-volatile must hold the first instructions, or the machine could never start.
A small amount of very fast SRAM between the CPU and main memory, holding recently and frequently used data so the CPU waits less often.

cards.q: Put registers, cache, RAM and secondary storage in order of speed.
cards.a: Registers (fastest, smallest, dearest), then cache, then RAM, then secondary storage (slowest, largest, cheapest). Speed, cost per bit and capacity all trade against each other.

cards.q: What is a cache hit and a cache miss?
cards.a: A **hit** is finding the wanted data already in cache. A **miss** means fetching it from slower memory — and the delay of a miss is why hit rate matters so much.
The observation that programs tend to reuse the same data soon (**temporal**) and to use data stored nearby (**spatial**). Caching only works because this is true.
Using part of secondary storage as though it were extra RAM, so programs larger than physical memory can run. Far slower, because the disc is involved.
When there is so little real RAM that the machine spends most of its time swapping pages in and out of virtual memory rather than doing useful work.

cards.q: Why not build a computer entirely from registers?
cards.a: Cost and physics. Register-speed storage needs about six transistors per bit and must sit close to the CPU; a machine with gigabytes of it would be unaffordable and too large to stay fast.

practice.q: Compare RAM and ROM, referring to volatility, whether they can be written to, and their typical use.
points: RAM is volatile, losing its contents when power is removed; ROM is non-volatile and retains them.
RAM can be read and written freely during normal operation.
ROM cannot be written to in normal use, or only through a special procedure.
RAM holds running programs and their data; ROM holds start-up instructions or firmware.

practice.q: Explain why a computer cannot start up with RAM alone.
points: RAM is volatile, so at power-on it contains nothing usable.
The processor must have instructions to fetch immediately, before any software has been loaded.
Those first instructions must therefore be held in non-volatile memory such as ROM.

practice.q: Explain how cache memory improves performance, using the terms hit, miss and locality of reference.
points: Cache holds copies of recently or frequently accessed data and instructions.
A hit means the CPU finds what it needs in cache and avoids the much slower main memory access.
Programs display locality of reference, reusing the same data and data stored nearby, so hits are common.
A miss costs the full main-memory access, so overall benefit depends on the hit rate being high.

practice.q: A computer has a cache with a hit rate of 90%. A cache access takes 2 ns and a main memory access takes 60 ns. Calculate the average access time and comment on the result.
points: Average $= 0.9 \times 2 + 0.1 \times 60$.
This is far closer to cache speed than to memory speed, despite one access in ten missing.
The remaining 10% of accesses contribute most of the time, so raising the hit rate further has a large effect.

practice.q: Explain why the memory in a computer is arranged as a hierarchy rather than as a single type.
points: Fast memory is expensive per bit and cannot be provided in large quantities affordably.
Large cheap memory is slow, and using it alone would leave the processor waiting.
A hierarchy gives a small amount of fast memory in front of a large amount of slow memory, approaching the speed of the first at close to the cost of the second.

practice.q: Explain what virtual memory is and describe one drawback of relying on it.
points: Part of secondary storage is used as though it were additional RAM.
Pages of data are moved between RAM and the disc as they are needed, so programs larger than physical memory can run.
Secondary storage is orders of magnitude slower than RAM, so performance drops when it is used heavily.
In the extreme the system thrashes, spending most of its time swapping rather than doing useful work.

practice.q: A laptop with 8 GB of RAM becomes very slow when several large applications are open. Explain what is happening and evaluate two possible responses.
points: The combined demand exceeds physical RAM, so the operating system moves pages to virtual memory on the disc.
Access to swapped pages is far slower than RAM, and in the worst case the machine thrashes.
Installing more RAM addresses the cause directly and lets more of the working set stay in memory.
Closing applications reduces demand immediately and costs nothing, but limits what the user can do at once.
A reasoned judgement is given, for example that more RAM is the better long-term fix if the workload is genuinely needed.

pages.title: Binary, denary and hexadecimal
pages.lede: Counting in a base other than ten, why machines count in two, and why programmers write in sixteen.

cards.q: What is the base of a number system?
cards.a: How many distinct digits it uses, and therefore the multiplier between one column and the next. Base 10 uses $0$–$9$; base 2 uses $0$–$1$; base 16 uses $0$–$F$.

cards.q: What is the place value of each column in binary?
cards.a: Powers of two, rising right to left: $1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128$.

cards.q: How do you convert denary to binary?
cards.a: Repeatedly divide by 2 and record the remainders, then read them **bottom to top**. Or subtract the largest power of two that fits, and repeat.
One hex digit is exactly four bits, so a byte is exactly two hex digits. It is far shorter than binary to write and far less error-prone to read, with no loss of information.

cards.q: What are the hex digits above 9?
How do you convert binary to hex quickly?
cards.a: Split into groups of four bits from the right, then write each group as one hex digit. $1011\,0110_2 = \text{B6}_{16}$.
Four bits — half a byte, and exactly one hexadecimal digit.

cards.q: How many values can $n$ bits represent?
cards.a: $2^n$. Eight bits give $2^8 = 256$ values, that is $0$ to $255$.

cards.q: What is the difference between a kilobyte and a kibibyte?
cards.a: $1\,\text{kB} = 1000$ bytes; $1\,\text{KiB} = 1024$ bytes. Memory is counted in powers of two, storage is usually sold in powers of ten.

practice.q: Convert the binary number $1101\,0011_2$ to denary, showing your working.
points: Place values identified as $128 + 64 + 16 + 2 + 1$.
Correct answer $211$.

practice.q: Convert the denary number $173$ to binary, showing your method.
points: A valid method is shown, either repeated division by 2 or subtraction of descending powers of two.
Working is correct at each step.
Correct answer $1010\,1101_2$.

practice.q: Convert $\text{9C}_{16}$ to denary.
points: $9 \times 16 = 144$ and $\text{C} = 12$.
Correct answer $156$.

practice.q: Explain why hexadecimal is used by programmers in preference to binary, when the machine itself uses neither.
points: One hex digit corresponds exactly to four bits, so conversion is direct and needs no arithmetic.
Hex is about a quarter the length of the equivalent binary, so it is quicker to write and easier to read without losing a digit.
No information is lost or approximated, unlike denary, where the correspondence to bits is not direct.

practice.q: A colour is stored as three bytes, one each for red, green and blue. Calculate how many distinct colours can be represented, and express the colour $\text{FF}\,\text{8C}\,00_{16}$ as three denary values.
points: Each byte gives $2^8 = 256$ levels.
$\text{FF} = 255$ and $\text{8C} = 140$.
So red $255$, green $140$, blue $0$.

practice.q: A file is described as 2 MB by its creator but shows as 1.91 MB in a file manager. Explain why.
points: One uses powers of ten, where $1\,\text{MB} = 1{,}000{,}000$ bytes.
The other uses powers of two, where the unit is $1{,}048{,}576$ bytes.
$2{,}000{,}000 \div 1{,}048{,}576 \approx 1.91$, so both figures describe the same file.

practice.q: A system uses 12 bits to store an unsigned integer. State the range of values it can hold, and explain what happens if the program tries to store 5000.
points: $2^{12} = 4096$ possible values.
Range is $0$ to $4095$ inclusive.
$5000$ exceeds the maximum, so it cannot be represented in 12 bits.
The value overflows and the stored result is wrong, typically wrapping round rather than raising an error.

pages.title: Negative numbers and two's complement
pages.lede: How to write a minus sign using only zeros and ones, and why the obvious method was abandoned for a stranger one that makes subtraction free.

cards.a: Use the leftmost bit as a sign ($0$ positive, $1$ negative) and the rest as the size. Simple to read, but it gives two zeros and needs separate circuitry for subtraction.

cards.q: Why was sign and magnitude abandoned?
cards.a: It has $+0$ and $-0$, wasting a pattern and complicating comparisons, and adding a positive to a negative needs a special subtractor rather than the ordinary adder.

cards.q: How do you form the two's complement of a binary number?
cards.a: **Invert every bit, then add one.** Equivalently, copy bits from the right up to and including the first $1$, then invert everything to the left of it.

cards.q: What is the range of an $n$-bit two's complement number?
cards.a: $-2^{n-1}$ to $+2^{n-1}-1$. For eight bits that is $-128$ to $+127$.

cards.q: Why is the negative range one larger than the positive?
cards.a: There is only one zero, so the $2^n$ patterns split into zero, $2^{n-1}-1$ positives and $2^{n-1}$ negatives.

cards.q: How do you read a negative two's complement number back to denary?
cards.a: Either apply invert-and-add-one again and negate the result, or treat the leading column as negative: in eight bits it is worth $-128$ rather than $+128$.

cards.q: Why does two's complement make subtraction free?
cards.a: Because $a - b$ is just $a + (-b)$, and negation is invert-and-add-one. One adder circuit handles both operations, so no subtractor is needed.

cards.q: How do you detect overflow in two's complement addition?
cards.a: When two numbers of the **same** sign produce a result of the **opposite** sign. Adding a positive to a negative can never overflow.

cards.q: What is an arithmetic shift left, and what does it do to the value?
cards.a: Shift every bit left one place and put a $0$ in at the right. It multiplies by two, provided the value does not overflow.

cards.q: What is an arithmetic shift right?
cards.a: Shift right and copy the **sign bit** into the vacated position, so negatives stay negative. It divides by two, rounding towards negative infinity.

practice.q: Convert $-53$ to 8-bit two's complement, showing your working.
points: Adding one gives $1100\,1011_2$.

practice.q: The 8-bit two's complement value $1001\,0110_2$ is stored. State its denary value.
points: Recognises the leading $1$ as negative and applies a correct method.
Correct answer $-106$.

practice.q: State the range of values that can be stored in a 16-bit two's complement integer, and explain how the range is derived.
points: There are $2^{16} = 65{,}536$ patterns available.
Half represent negatives and half zero-or-positive, giving $-2^{15}$ to $+2^{15}-1$.

practice.q: Explain why two's complement is used in preference to sign and magnitude.
points: Sign and magnitude produces two representations of zero, wasting a pattern and complicating equality tests.
Two's complement has a single zero.
In two's complement, subtraction can be performed by negating and adding.
One adder circuit therefore performs both addition and subtraction, reducing hardware cost and complexity.
