practice.q: A librarian wants a list of every book that has never been borrowed. Explain how you would write this query and why a simple inner join will not work.
points: An inner join between Book and Loan only returns books that appear in Loan.
Books never borrowed have no matching Loan row, so they are excluded — the very rows wanted.
A LEFT JOIN from Book to Loan keeps every book, with nulls where there is no loan.
Adding WHERE Loan.LoanID IS NULL then keeps only the unborrowed ones.
An equivalent correct approach using NOT IN or NOT EXISTS is also credited.

pages.title: Transactions and other kinds of database
pages.lede: Making several changes count as one, what happens when two people change the same row at once, and when the relational model is the wrong tool.

cards.a: A group of operations treated as a **single indivisible unit** — either all of them take effect, or none do.

cards.q: What do the letters ACID stand for?
cards.a: **Atomicity**, **Consistency**, **Isolation**, **Durability**.
A transaction happens completely or not at all. A failure part-way is rolled back, leaving no trace.
A transaction moves the database from one valid state to another, never leaving integrity rules broken.
Concurrent transactions do not see each other's partial work; the result is as if they had run one after another.
Once a transaction is committed, it survives a crash or power loss, because it has been written to non-volatile storage.
Undoing every change made by a transaction that could not complete, returning the database to its state beforehand.
Two transactions each holding a lock the other needs, so neither can proceed. One must be aborted to break it.

cards.q: What is the lost update problem?
cards.a: Two transactions read the same value, both modify it, and the second write overwrites the first — so one update vanishes.
One that does not use the relational table model — document, key-value, column-family or graph — usually trading strict consistency for scale and flexibility.

cards.q: When is a document database a better fit than a relational one?
cards.a: When records vary in structure, when the schema changes often, or when data is always read as a whole rather than joined across tables.
A large store of historical data assembled from several systems for analysis, usually denormalised and optimised for reading rather than updating.

practice.q: Explain what is meant by atomicity and durability, using a bank transfer as your example.
points: Atomicity means the whole transaction takes effect or none of it does.
In a transfer, the debit and the credit must both happen, or neither, so money is never lost or created.
Durability means that once committed, the change survives a subsequent failure.
The completed transfer must still be there after a power cut, because it was written to non-volatile storage before the commit was confirmed.

practice.q: Explain the lost update problem.
points: Two transactions read the same value at about the same time.
Each calculates a new value from what it read and writes it back.
The second write overwrites the first, so one of the updates is lost even though both appeared to succeed.

practice.q: Explain what a deadlock is and describe one way a database system can deal with it.
points: Two transactions each hold a lock that the other is waiting for.
Neither can release its lock until it has acquired the other, so both wait indefinitely.
The system detects the cycle, for example with a wait-for graph or a timeout.
It then aborts and rolls back one transaction, allowing the other to continue; the aborted one can be retried.

practice.q: Explain why isolation matters when many users access a database at once.
points: Without isolation, one transaction can read another's partially completed work.
Decisions made on that intermediate data may be wrong if the other transaction is later rolled back.
Isolation makes the outcome equivalent to running the transactions one after another, so results are predictable.

practice.q: Compare a relational database with a document database.
points: A relational database stores data in tables with a fixed schema and enforced relationships.
It guarantees integrity and supports flexible querying across tables using joins.
A document database stores self-contained records that may differ in structure, with no fixed schema.
It scales more easily and suits varying or rapidly changing data, but consistency and cross-record querying are weaker.

practice.q: An online shop's product catalogue has items with wildly differing attributes — books have authors, clothes have sizes, electronics have voltages. Discuss whether a document database would suit it.
points: A relational schema would need either many sparse columns or a separate table per product type.
A document database lets each product carry only the attributes it has.
Products are usually retrieved whole, so the lack of joins costs little.
However reporting across product types, and enforcing rules such as valid prices, become the application's responsibility.

practice.q: A hospital is choosing a database for patient records. Discuss whether ACID guarantees should be prioritised over scalability.
points: Patient records are safety-critical, so an incorrect or partially applied update could cause harm.
Atomicity ensures related changes, such as a prescription and its dose, cannot be half applied.
Durability ensures a recorded treatment is not lost in a failure.
Hospital data volumes are large but not at the scale where relational systems fail, so the scalability argument is weak here.
A clear judgement in favour of ACID is reached and justified by consequence of error.

pages.title: What machine learning is
pages.lede: Programs that are not written but fitted, why anyone would want that, and the three ways of learning you are expected to tell apart.

cards.a: Building a program by **fitting it to examples** rather than writing its rules by hand. The rules are found by the fitting process, not by a programmer.

cards.q: When is machine learning the right approach?
cards.a: When the rules are real but nobody can state them — recognising a face, spotting spam — and plenty of examples exist.

cards.q: When is machine learning the wrong approach?
cards.a: When the rules are already known and exact. Nobody should learn payroll tax from examples; it is written down and must be exactly right.
Learning from examples that come with the **right answers** attached, so the model learns a mapping from input to a known output.
Learning from data with **no labels**, finding structure — usually groups — that nobody specified in advance.
Learning by acting and receiving a **reward or penalty**, with no correct answer given, only a signal about how well it went.
One measurable property used as input — a pixel value, a word count, an age. The set of features is what the model actually sees.
The correct output for a training example. Only supervised learning has them, and producing them is usually the expensive part.
The thing produced by training: a set of numbers, plus a rule for turning an input into an output using them.
Adjusting the model's numbers so that its outputs on the training data get closer to the labels.

cards.q: Why must test data be kept separate from training data?
cards.a: Because a model can score well on data it has already seen without having learned anything general. Only unseen data measures that.

cards.q: What is the difference between a rule-based program and a learned model?
cards.a: A rule-based program's behaviour is stated by a person and can be read. A learned model's behaviour is fitted from data, and often nobody can say why it decides as it does.

practice.q: Explain what distinguishes machine learning from traditional programming.
points: In traditional programming a person writes explicit rules that produce the output from the input.
In machine learning the rules are derived automatically by fitting a model to example data.
The programmer supplies the data and the structure of the model, rather than the decision logic itself.

practice.q: Give one problem for which machine learning is appropriate and one for which it is not, justifying both.
points: An appropriate problem is identified, such as recognising handwriting or detecting spam.
It is justified because the rules are genuinely too complex or subtle to state, but examples are plentiful.
An inappropriate problem is identified, such as calculating tax or validating a password.
It is justified because the rules are already known exactly and an approximate answer would be unacceptable.

practice.q: Distinguish between supervised and unsupervised learning, giving an example of each.
points: Supervised learning uses training data in which each example is paired with the correct answer.
An example is classifying email as spam or not spam, using messages already marked by users.
Unsupervised learning uses data with no correct answers supplied.
An example is grouping customers by purchasing behaviour, where the groups are not known in advance.

practice.q: Explain what reinforcement learning is and how it differs from supervised learning.
points: The system takes actions in an environment and receives a reward or penalty for the outcome.
It is never told what the correct action was, only how good the result turned out to be.
Supervised learning is given the correct answer for each example, so it can be corrected directly.

practice.q: Explain the terms feature and label, using a system that predicts house prices as your example.
points: A feature is a measurable input property, such as floor area, number of bedrooms or postcode.
A label is the correct output for a training example, here the price the house actually sold for.
The model learns a relationship from the features to the label, so unlabelled houses can be priced.

practice.q: Explain why a model's accuracy must be measured on data it was not trained on.
points: A model can achieve high accuracy simply by memorising the training examples.
Memorising does not produce correct answers on anything new, which is what the model is for.
Held-back test data has not influenced training, so performance on it estimates real-world performance.
Without that separation, the reported accuracy is misleadingly high.

practice.q: A school proposes using machine learning to predict which students are at risk of failing. Discuss whether this is appropriate.
points: Patterns in attendance, grades and engagement are plausibly predictive but hard to state as rules, so the technique fits.
Historical student data provides labelled examples, since past outcomes are known.
However predictions may reflect bias in past data, disadvantaging groups already treated unfairly.
A prediction may become self-fulfilling if staff treat flagged students differently.
A reasoned conclusion is reached, for example that it is defensible only as a prompt for human review rather than as a decision.

pages.title: Supervised learning and how it fails
pages.lede: Classification, regression, and the two ways a model can be wrong that have nothing to do with the algorithm being bad.

cards.a: Supervised learning where the output is a **category** — spam or not spam, which digit, which species.
Supervised learning where the output is a **number on a continuous scale** — a price, a temperature, a time.

cards.q: What is a training set, and what is a test set?
cards.a: The **training set** is used to fit the model. The **test set** is held back and used only once, to estimate how it will perform on data it has never seen.
When a model learns the noise and quirks of the training data rather than the general pattern. It scores well on training data and badly on anything new.
When a model is too simple to capture the real pattern, so it does badly on training and test data alike.
Training accuracy keeps rising while test accuracy stops rising and then falls. The **gap** between them is the symptom.

cards.q: Name three ways to reduce overfitting.
cards.a: More training data, a simpler model, or stopping training earlier. Removing irrelevant features also helps.
A table of true positives, false positives, true negatives and false negatives, showing not just how often the model is wrong but **how** it is wrong.
The model said yes and the truth was no — a legitimate email marked as spam, a healthy patient told they are ill.
The model said no and the truth was yes — spam reaching the inbox, an illness missed.

cards.q: Why can accuracy be a misleading measure?
cards.a: On imbalanced data it rewards ignoring the rare class. If 1 in 1000 transactions is fraud, always answering "not fraud" is 99.9% accurate and useless.
**Precision** is how many of the flagged cases were real. **Recall** is how many of the real cases were flagged. Raising one usually lowers the other.

practice.q: Distinguish between classification and regression, giving an example of each.
points: Classification predicts which of a set of discrete categories an input belongs to.
An example is deciding whether an email is spam, or which handwritten digit an image shows.
Regression predicts a continuous numeric value, such as a house price or tomorrow's temperature.

practice.q: Explain what overfitting is and how it can be detected.
points: The model learns detail and noise specific to the training data rather than the underlying pattern.
It therefore performs very well on training data but poorly on new data.
It is detected by evaluating on a separate test set that was not used in training.
A widening gap between training accuracy and test accuracy indicates overfitting.

practice.q: State three ways of reducing overfitting.
points: Provide more training data, so the noise averages out relative to the real pattern.
Use a simpler model with fewer parameters, so it cannot memorise individual examples.
Stop training earlier, or remove irrelevant features, so it fits less closely to the training set.

practice.q: A medical screening model is 99% accurate on a population where 1% have the disease. Explain why this figure is not reassuring.
points: A model that always predicted "no disease" would also be 99% accurate.
Accuracy therefore says nothing about whether the rare positive cases are being found.
The model might be missing every genuine case, which is precisely the failure that matters.
Recall, or the number of false negatives, should be reported instead of, or as well as, accuracy.

practice.q: Explain the difference between a false positive and a false negative, and give a situation where each is the more serious.
points: A false positive is a case wrongly flagged as belonging to the class of interest.
A false negative is a genuine case that the model failed to flag.
A false negative is more serious in disease screening, where a missed illness goes untreated.
A false positive is more serious in an automatic spam filter that deletes mail, where a real message is lost.

practice.q: Explain what precision and recall measure and why improving one usually worsens the other.
points: Precision is the proportion of flagged cases that were genuinely positive.
Recall is the proportion of genuinely positive cases that were flagged.
Lowering the threshold flags more cases, catching more real ones but also more wrong ones.
Recall therefore rises while precision falls, and the balance must be chosen to suit the consequences of each error.

practice.q: A bank is building a fraud detection model. Discuss how it should decide the balance between false positives and false negatives.
points: A false negative means fraud goes undetected and money is lost.
A false positive means a legitimate transaction is blocked, inconveniencing a customer.
The costs are not equal and are not purely financial — repeated false blocks damage trust and may lose customers.
A sensible design flags borderline cases for human review rather than deciding automatically.
A reasoned position is reached, weighing the cost of each error type for this specific application.

pages.title: Unsupervised learning
pages.lede: Finding structure nobody labelled, why there is no right answer to check against, and how k-means actually works.

cards.a: Grouping data points so that those in a group are more similar to each other than to those in other groups. No group is defined in advance.
Segmenting customers by behaviour, grouping documents by topic, spotting which readings do not fit any group.
Place $k$ centres, assign each point to its nearest centre, move each centre to the mean of its points, and repeat until nothing moves.

cards.q: What does the $k$ in k-means stand for?
cards.a: The number of clusters, which you must choose **before** running it. The algorithm will not tell you the right number.

cards.q: Why can k-means give different answers on the same data?
cards.a: It starts from randomly placed centres and settles on the nearest good arrangement, which is not always the best one.

cards.q: How is the quality of a clustering judged?
cards.a: By how tight the clusters are and how far apart, and ultimately by whether the groups are useful to a person. There is no correct answer to compare with.
Finding points that fit no cluster or lie far from all of them — used for fraud, faults and intrusions.
Reducing many features to a few that carry most of the variation, making data easier to visualise, store and learn from.

cards.q: Why must features be scaled before clustering?
cards.a: Distance is dominated by whichever feature has the largest numeric range. Income in pounds would swamp age in years.
Plotting cluster tightness against $k$ and choosing the point where improvement suddenly slows — the bend in the curve.

cards.q: Why is unsupervised learning harder to evaluate than supervised?
cards.a: There are no labels, so there is nothing to be right or wrong about. Judgement about usefulness replaces measurement.

practice.q: Explain what clustering is and give one practical use.
points: Data points are grouped so that members of a group are more similar to each other than to members of other groups.
The groups are discovered from the data rather than specified in advance.
A valid use is given, such as segmenting customers, grouping documents by topic, or detecting unusual behaviour.

practice.q: Describe the steps of the k-means algorithm.
points: Choose $k$ and place $k$ cluster centres, usually at random positions or random data points.
Assign every data point to the nearest centre.
Move each centre to the mean position of the points assigned to it.
Repeat the assignment and update steps until the assignments stop changing.

practice.q: Explain why running k-means twice on identical data can produce different clusters.
points: The initial centre positions are chosen randomly.
The algorithm converges to a locally good arrangement rather than a guaranteed best one.
Different starting positions can therefore lead to different final clusterings, so it is usually run several times.

practice.q: A dataset contains age in years and income in pounds. Explain why the data should be scaled before clustering, and what happens if it is not.
points: Clustering assigns points by distance between them.
Income values are numerically thousands of times larger than ages.
Distance is therefore dominated almost entirely by income, and age has effectively no influence.
Scaling each feature to a comparable range lets both contribute to the grouping.

practice.q: Explain what the elbow method is used for and how it works.
points: It is used to choose a sensible value of $k$, which the algorithm cannot determine itself.
A measure of within-cluster spread is plotted against increasing $k$.
The value at which further increases stop reducing spread substantially — the bend — is chosen.

practice.q: Explain why evaluating an unsupervised model is harder than evaluating a supervised one.
points: Supervised learning has labels, so predictions can be compared with known correct answers.
Unsupervised learning has no labels, so there is nothing to compare against.
Numeric measures of cluster tightness and separation exist but do not establish that the grouping is meaningful.
Ultimately a person must judge whether the discovered groups are useful for the purpose intended.

practice.q: A supermarket wants to group its customers to target offers. Discuss how it should approach this and what could go wrong.
points: Features should be chosen that reflect purchasing behaviour, such as spend, frequency and category mix.
Features must be scaled so that no single one dominates the distance calculation.
$k$ must be chosen deliberately, for example by the elbow method, and the resulting groups inspected by staff.
The groups may encode something unintended, such as income proxies, leading to unfair or intrusive targeting.
A reasoned conclusion is reached about validating the groups before acting on them.

pages.title: Neural networks, bias and responsibility
pages.lede: What a neuron actually computes, why depth helps, and the ways a technically correct model can still do harm.

cards.a: A unit that multiplies each input by a **weight**, adds them up with a **bias**, and passes the total through an **activation function**.

cards.q: Write down what a neuron computes.
cards.a: $y = f\left(\sum_i w_i x_i + b\right)$, where $f$ is the activation function.
A number saying how much one input matters to this neuron. Weights are what training adjusts.

cards.q: What is an activation function, and why is one needed?
cards.a: A non-linear function applied to the neuron's total. Without it, any stack of layers collapses into a single linear function and depth buys nothing.

cards.q: Name the three kinds of layer.
cards.a: **Input** — one unit per feature. **Hidden** — the layers in between, where the work happens. **Output** — one unit per thing being predicted.
A single number measuring how wrong the network's outputs are on the training data. Training is the search for weights that make it small.
Working out how much each weight contributed to the loss, by pushing the error backwards through the layers, so every weight can be nudged in the right direction.
Repeatedly adjusting every weight a small step in the direction that reduces the loss.
How big those steps are. Too small and training crawls; too large and it overshoots and never settles.
One complete pass through the whole training set.

cards.q: Where does bias in a model come from?
cards.a: From the data. A model trained on past decisions reproduces the patterns in those decisions, including the unfair ones.

cards.q: What is the black box problem?
cards.a: A trained network's behaviour lives in millions of weights, so it can be tested but not read. Nobody can say **why** it decided as it did.

practice.q: Describe what a single artificial neuron computes.
points: Each input is multiplied by its own weight.
The weighted inputs are summed, and a bias term is added.
The total is passed through an activation function.
The result of that function is the neuron's output, which may feed other neurons.

practice.q: Explain why a neural network needs non-linear activation functions.
points: Without them each layer computes a linear combination of its inputs.
A linear function of a linear function is itself linear.
Any number of layers would therefore be equivalent to a single layer.
Non-linearity allows the network to represent relationships a straight line cannot, which is the point of adding depth.

practice.q: Describe how a neural network is trained.
points: Training examples are passed forwards through the network to produce outputs.
A loss function measures how far those outputs are from the correct labels.
Backpropagation determines how much each weight contributed to the loss.
Each weight is adjusted by a small step in the direction that reduces the loss, and the process repeats for many epochs.

practice.q: Explain the effect of setting the learning rate too high and too low.
points: Too low, and the weights change very slowly, so training takes an impractical amount of time.
Too high, and the steps overshoot the minimum.
The loss then oscillates or grows rather than settling, so the network may never converge.

practice.q: A recruitment model trained on ten years of past hiring decisions rejects more female applicants. Explain how this happened and what should be done.
points: The training data records past human decisions, which were themselves biased.
The model learned to reproduce those patterns, since matching the historical labels is exactly what it was optimised to do.
Removing the gender field is insufficient, because other features correlate with it and act as proxies.
Outcomes should be audited across groups, and the system should support rather than replace human decisions.

practice.q: Explain what is meant by the black box problem and why it matters.
points: A trained network's behaviour is distributed across a very large number of weights with no individual meaning.
It is therefore possible to test what it does but not to read why it did it.
In consequential decisions such as credit, medicine or justice, the affected person cannot be given a reason.
This makes errors hard to challenge and may conflict with a legal right to an explanation.

practice.q: A hospital proposes replacing an initial diagnostic assessment with a neural network that outperforms junior doctors on test data. Discuss whether it should.
points: Better measured performance is a genuine argument, since missed diagnoses cause harm.
However test performance may not transfer, if the deployment population differs from the training data.
The model cannot explain its reasoning, so a clinician cannot check it or a patient challenge it.
Responsibility for a wrong diagnosis becomes unclear when no person made the decision.
A reasoned conclusion is reached, for example that it should advise rather than decide, with human sign-off retained.

pages.title: Abstraction and decomposition
pages.lede: The two habits that make a problem too big to hold in your head into one you can actually write down.

cards.a: Framing a problem so that a computer can carry out the solution — breaking it up, spotting what repeats, ignoring what does not matter, and writing precise steps.
Breaking a problem into smaller sub-problems that can be solved, tested and understood on their own.

cards.q: Why is decomposition useful beyond making a problem smaller?
cards.a: Each part can be tested separately, written by a different person, and replaced without disturbing the rest.
Deliberately ignoring detail that does not matter for the problem in hand, so what remains can be reasoned about.

cards.q: Give an everyday example of abstraction.
cards.a: A map of the underground. It gets the connections right and the distances deliberately wrong, because a passenger needs the order of stations, not the geography.
One whose hidden detail becomes visible when something goes wrong — a file that behaves like local storage until the network drops.
Noticing that parts of a problem repeat, or resemble a problem already solved, so one solution can serve several places.
Expressing a solution as a sequence of unambiguous steps that always terminates and always gives the intended result.

cards.q: What is an interface, in the sense used here?
cards.a: The agreed boundary of a component: what it takes in and gives back, with nothing said about how it does it.

cards.q: Why does hiding the implementation matter?
cards.a: Anything hidden can be changed without breaking the callers. Anything exposed becomes something you must keep working forever.
Starting from the whole problem and repeatedly splitting it into parts, until each part is small enough to write directly.

practice.q: Explain what is meant by decomposition and why it is useful when developing a large program.
points: A problem is broken down into smaller sub-problems that can be solved individually.
Each part is small enough to be understood, written and tested on its own.
Parts can be developed in parallel by different people, and one can be replaced without rewriting the others.

practice.q: Explain what abstraction is, using an example, and state one risk of it.
points: Abstraction means removing or hiding detail that is not relevant to the problem being solved.
A valid example is given, such as a underground map, a function signature, or a file system hiding disc blocks.
It allows the remaining structure to be reasoned about without being overwhelmed by detail.
The risk is that hidden detail can still matter, so behaviour becomes surprising when the abstraction leaks.

practice.q: A student is asked to write a program that manages a school library. Describe how they should decompose the problem.
points: Identify the major areas of responsibility, such as members, the catalogue, loans and reporting.
Break each area into specific operations, for example adding a member, searching the catalogue, issuing a loan.
Define what each operation takes in and gives back, so parts can be written independently.
Identify shared sub-problems, such as validating a date, that can be written once and reused.

practice.q: Explain what pattern recognition means in computational thinking and why it saves work.
points: It means noticing that parts of a problem repeat, or resemble something already solved.
The repeated part can then be written once as a function or loop rather than many times.
Fixing a fault in that one place fixes it everywhere it is used.

practice.q: Explain the difference between what a component does and how it does it, and why the distinction matters.
points: What it does is its interface — the inputs it accepts and the results it produces.
How it does it is the implementation, which is hidden from anything that uses it.
The implementation can then be changed or improved without affecting any caller.
If callers depend on internal detail, that detail can no longer be changed, and the component becomes fixed in place.

practice.q: A program stores a list of student names and must find whether a given name is present. Identify the sub-problems and state which detail can be abstracted away.
points: Sub-problems include reading the list, comparing a name against an entry, and reporting the result.
Comparison must handle differences such as case or trailing spaces, which is a sub-problem of its own.
How the list is stored can be abstracted away — the search does not need to know it is an array rather than a file.
This means the storage could later change without altering the searching code.

practice.q: Discuss the claim that abstraction always makes a program easier to work with.
points: Abstraction reduces the amount that must be held in mind at once, which genuinely helps on large systems.
It allows implementations to be replaced without disturbing callers.
However each layer adds indirection, so tracing what actually happens becomes harder.
A leaky abstraction can mislead, because behaviour depends on detail the interface promised to hide.
A reasoned conclusion is reached, for example that abstraction helps in proportion to how reliably the hidden detail stays hidden.

pages.title: Algorithms, flowcharts and pseudocode
pages.lede: Writing a method down precisely enough that somebody else could follow it, and the three notations the exam expects.

cards.a: A finite sequence of unambiguous steps that takes an input and produces the intended output.

cards.q: Name the four properties every algorithm must have.
cards.a: **Finite** — it ends. **Unambiguous** — each step has one meaning. **Defined input and output**. **Effective** — every step can actually be carried out.
A way of writing an algorithm in structured English, precise about logic but free of the syntax of any particular language.

cards.q: Why use pseudocode rather than real code in a design?
cards.a: It keeps attention on the method rather than the syntax, and it can be read by someone who does not know the language you will use.

cards.q: What are the three control structures?
cards.a: **Sequence** — one step after another. **Selection** — choose a branch. **Iteration** — repeat. Every algorithm is built from these three.

cards.q: What does a rectangle mean in a flowchart?
cards.a: A process — a step that does something.

cards.q: What does a diamond mean in a flowchart?
cards.a: A decision. It has one way in and two ways out, labelled with the conditions.

cards.q: What do the rounded ends of a flowchart mean?
cards.a: Terminals — where the algorithm starts and where it stops.

cards.q: What is a parallelogram in a flowchart?
cards.a: Input or output.
A table with one column per variable and one row per step, recording how the values change as an algorithm runs.
Running a loop one time too many or too few, usually from confusing "up to" with "up to and including". It is the commonest bug in this topic.
Working through an algorithm by hand with chosen values, usually recorded in a trace table, to check it does what you think.

practice.q: State the four properties an algorithm must have, explaining one of them.
points: It must be finite, terminating after a limited number of steps.
It must be unambiguous, so each step has exactly one interpretation.
It must have defined inputs and outputs.
Each step must be effective, meaning it can actually be carried out; one of the four is explained.

practice.q: Write pseudocode for an algorithm that reads 10 numbers and outputs the largest.
points: A variable is initialised to hold the largest so far, either from the first input or a suitable starting value.
A loop repeats the correct number of times.
Each input is compared with the largest so far and replaces it when greater.
The result is output after the loop, not inside it.

practice.q: State what each of these flowchart symbols means: rectangle, diamond, parallelogram.
points: Rectangle — a process, a step that does something.
Diamond — a decision, with two labelled exits.
Parallelogram — input or output.

practice.q: Complete a trace table for the following algorithm with input 4. `total ← 0; count ← 1; WHILE count ≤ n DO total ← total + count; count ← count + 1; ENDWHILE; OUTPUT total`
points: Table has columns for count, total and the condition.
Rows show total taking values 1, 3, 6 then 10.
Count reaches 5 and the condition becomes false.
The output is 10.

practice.q: Explain what an off-by-one error is and give an example.
points: The loop executes one time too many, or one time too few.
It typically arises from confusing "less than" with "less than or equal to", or from counting from 0 rather than 1.
A valid example is given, such as a loop over an array of length $n$ using indices 1 to $n$ and reading past the end.

practice.q: Explain why an algorithm should be designed before code is written.
points: The logic can be checked and corrected before effort is spent on syntax.
Errors found at the design stage are far cheaper to fix than errors found in working code.
The design can be reviewed by others, including those who do not know the language.
The same design can then be implemented in any language.

practice.q: A student writes an algorithm to find the average of a list of numbers, but it crashes when the list is empty. Explain the problem and how designing with edge cases in mind would have prevented it.
points: The average is the total divided by the count, and with an empty list the count is zero.
Division by zero causes an error at run time rather than a wrong answer.
Considering edge cases means asking what happens at the extremes — empty, one item, very large — before writing code.
The design should specify what an empty list means, for example returning zero or reporting that there is no average.
A guard checking the count before dividing implements that decision.

pages.title: Variables, types and operators
pages.lede: What a variable really is, why a type is a promise rather than a label, and the operators that catch people out.

cards.a: A named location in memory holding a value that may change while the program runs.

cards.q: What is the difference between a variable and a constant?
cards.a: A constant is given a value once and may not be changed afterwards, which lets the compiler catch an accidental assignment.
A promise about what kind of value a name holds, which determines how the bits are interpreted and which operations are allowed.
**Integer**, **real** or float, **boolean**, **character**, and **string**.

cards.q: Why does an integer behave differently from a real?
cards.a: An integer is exact and has a fixed range; a real is stored as an approximation, so arithmetic on it accumulates small errors.
Types are fixed and checked before the program runs, so a mismatch is a compile error rather than a crash.
A value carries its type at run time and a name can hold any type. Flexible, but a mismatch is only found when that line executes.
Integer division, discarding the remainder. $7 // 2$ is $3$.

cards.q: What does the modulus operator do?
cards.a: Gives the remainder. $7 \bmod 2$ is $1$. It is how you test divisibility and how you wrap a value round a range.

cards.q: What is the difference between `=` and `==`?
cards.a: `=` **assigns** a value to a name. `==` **compares** two values and gives a boolean.
Converting a value from one type to another, such as the string `"42"` to the integer $42$.

cards.q: Why should you never compare two reals with `==`?
cards.a: They are approximations, so a calculation that should give $0.3$ may give $0.30000000000000004$. Compare the difference against a small tolerance instead.

practice.q: Explain what a variable is and how it differs from a constant.
points: A variable is a named location in memory that holds a value.
Its value can be changed while the program is running.
A constant is assigned once and cannot be changed, so an accidental reassignment is caught rather than silently accepted.

practice.q: Explain why data types are needed, referring to how values are stored.
points: The same bit pattern can mean different things, so something must say how to interpret it.
The type determines how much memory is allocated for the value.
It determines which operations are valid, so adding a number to a string can be rejected.
It allows errors to be detected, in some languages before the program is ever run.

practice.q: State the value and the type of each expression: `7 / 2`, `7 // 2`, `7 % 2`, `"7" + "2"` in Python.
points: `7 / 2` gives $3.5$, a real.
`7 // 2` gives $3$, an integer.
`7 % 2` gives $1$, an integer.
`"7" + "2"` gives `"72"`, a string, because + concatenates strings.

practice.q: Explain the difference between `=` and `==`, and describe an error caused by confusing them.
points: `=` assigns a value to a variable.
`==` compares two values and produces a boolean.
Writing `=` inside a condition either fails to compile or, in some languages, assigns and then tests the assigned value, so the condition is always true.

practice.q: Compare static and dynamic typing.
points: Static typing fixes each variable's type, which is checked before the program runs.
Type errors are therefore found at compile time, and the compiler can generate faster code.
Dynamic typing allows a name to hold any type, with checking done as each line executes.
This is quicker to write and more flexible, but a type error may not surface until the program is in use.

practice.q: A program calculates `0.1 + 0.2` and tests whether the result equals `0.3`. The test fails. Explain why, and state how the comparison should be written.
points: Reals are stored in binary as approximations, and $0.1$ and $0.2$ have no exact binary representation.
The sum is therefore very slightly different from $0.3$.
An exact equality test between reals will fail even though the values are conceptually equal.
The absolute difference should be compared against a small tolerance instead.

practice.q: A student stores a person's age as a string because it was read from a text box. Discuss the consequences and how they should handle it.
points: Arithmetic on the value will either fail or behave unexpectedly, since + concatenates strings.
Comparisons will be alphabetical rather than numeric, so "9" would sort after "10".
The input should be cast to an integer as soon as it is read.
The cast can fail if the text is not a number, so it must be validated or the failure handled.
Converting at the boundary means the rest of the program can rely on the value being a number.

pages.title: Selection and iteration
pages.lede: Choosing a branch and repeating a block — two of the three control structures, and where nearly every logic bug lives.

cards.a: Choosing which block to run based on a condition — `if`, `elif`, `else`.
An expression that evaluates to true or false, usually built from comparisons combined with `and`, `or` and `not`.

cards.q: What is the difference between a chain of `if`s and `if`/`elif`?
cards.a: Separate `if`s are all tested and several can run. An `if`/`elif` chain stops at the first match, so exactly one branch runs.
Putting one control structure inside another. Beyond two or three levels it becomes very hard to reason about.
Stopping as soon as the answer is known: `False and anything` is false without evaluating the second part. It lets you guard a test with the check that makes it safe.
One that repeats a known number of times — a `for` loop over a range or a collection.
One that repeats until a condition becomes false — a `while` loop. The number of iterations need not be known in advance.

cards.q: When should you use `while` rather than `for`?
cards.a: When you cannot say in advance how many repetitions are needed — reading until end of file, or retrying until a user gives valid input.
The condition never becoming false, usually because the variable it tests is never updated inside the loop.
`break` leaves the loop immediately. `continue` skips the rest of this iteration and starts the next.

cards.q: What is a nested loop, and what does it cost?
cards.a: A loop inside a loop. The body runs the product of the two counts, so two loops of $n$ run $n^2$ times.
A special value marking the end of input, such as $-1$ or an empty line, used to stop a condition-controlled loop.

practice.q: Explain the difference between using several separate `if` statements and using an `if`/`elif`/`else` chain.
points: Separate `if` statements are each evaluated, so more than one block can run.
An `if`/`elif` chain stops as soon as a condition is true, so exactly one block runs.
Using separate `if`s where the cases are mutually exclusive can cause several branches to run and produce a wrong result.

practice.q: Distinguish between a count-controlled and a condition-controlled loop, giving an example of when each is appropriate.
points: A count-controlled loop repeats a number of times known before it starts.
It suits processing every item of a list of known length.
A condition-controlled loop repeats until a condition becomes false, with the count unknown in advance.
It suits reading input until a sentinel value, or retrying until the user enters something valid.

practice.q: Explain what causes an infinite loop and how to avoid one.
points: The loop's condition never becomes false.
Usually the variable tested in the condition is never changed inside the loop body.
Ensure that every path through the body moves the state towards making the condition false.

practice.q: Explain what short-circuit evaluation is and give an example where it prevents an error.
points: Evaluation of a boolean expression stops as soon as the result is determined.
With `and`, a false first operand means the second is never evaluated.
A guard can therefore be placed first, such as checking a list is not empty before indexing it.
Written as `if len(items) > 0 and items[0] == x`, the index is never attempted on an empty list.

practice.q: A program uses a nested loop over two lists of 1000 items each. State how many times the inner body runs and explain the implication.
points: The body runs $1000 \times 1000 = 1{,}000{,}000$ times.
Running time grows with the product of the two lengths, not their sum.
Doubling both lists would make it four times slower.
For large data this becomes impractical, so a different approach such as a lookup structure may be needed.

practice.q: Write pseudocode that repeatedly asks for a mark between 0 and 100 until a valid one is entered.
points: A condition-controlled loop is used, since the number of attempts is unknown.
The input is read inside the loop.
The condition checks both bounds, rejecting values below 0 and above 100.
The loop exits only when the value is valid, and the value is available afterwards.

practice.q: A student's loop to find whether a value is in a list always reports "not found" even when it is present. Their code sets a flag to True on a match, but the `else` that sets it to False is inside the loop. Explain the fault and how to fix it.
points: The flag is reset on every iteration where the item does not match.
A match found early is therefore overwritten by the next non-matching item.
Only the last comparison affects the result, so it reports found only if the last item matches.
The flag should be initialised to False once, before the loop.
Inside the loop it should only ever be set to True, never back to False; breaking out on a match is also correct.

pages.title: Functions and collections
pages.lede: Naming a piece of work so it can be reused and tested, and the four ways of holding more than one thing at once.

cards.a: A named, reusable block of code that takes parameters and usually returns a result.

cards.q: Give three reasons to use functions.
cards.a: The code is written once and reused; each part can be tested on its own; and the name documents what the block does.

cards.q: What is the difference between a parameter and an argument?
cards.a: A **parameter** is the name in the definition. An **argument** is the actual value passed in at the call.
The result a function hands back to whatever called it. A function with no `return` gives back nothing.
The region of a program in which a name is visible. A variable made inside a function is local to it and gone when it ends.
Any part of the program can change one, so a wrong value could have come from anywhere. That makes a bug very hard to locate.
Anything a function does beyond returning a value — printing, writing a file, changing a global or mutating its argument.
An ordered, changeable collection accessed by position, allowing duplicates.

cards.q: What is a tuple, and when would you use one?
cards.a: An ordered collection that cannot be changed after creation. Use one for a fixed group of related values, such as a coordinate.
A collection of key–value pairs, looked up by key rather than by position. Keys are unique.
An unordered collection with no duplicates, fast at answering whether something is a member.

cards.q: Why is looking something up in a dictionary faster than searching a list?
cards.a: A list must be scanned item by item, taking time proportional to its length. A dictionary computes the key's position directly, so the time barely changes as it grows.

practice.q: Explain three benefits of dividing a program into functions.
points: Code written once can be called from many places, avoiding duplication.
A fault is fixed in one place rather than in every copy.
Each function can be tested independently of the rest of the program.
A well-chosen name documents what the block does, making the calling code readable.

practice.q: Explain the difference between a parameter and an argument, and between a local and a global variable.
points: A parameter is the name given in the function definition; an argument is the value supplied when it is called.
A local variable exists only inside the function and is destroyed when it returns.
A global variable is visible throughout the program and persists between calls.

practice.q: Explain why heavy use of global variables makes a program harder to maintain.
points: Any part of the program can modify a global, so the source of a wrong value is not localised.
A function's behaviour then depends on state that is not visible in its parameters.
It cannot be tested in isolation, because it depends on the surrounding program's state.
Two parts of the program may use the same global for different purposes, causing interference.

practice.q: Compare a list and a dictionary, stating when each is the better choice.
points: A list is ordered and accessed by numeric position, allowing duplicates.
A dictionary stores key–value pairs and is accessed by key, which must be unique.
A list suits data with a meaningful order, or that is processed in sequence.
A dictionary suits looking a value up by a natural identifier, and does so far faster than searching a list.

practice.q: Explain why a tuple might be used instead of a list.
points: A tuple cannot be changed after it is created.
This prevents accidental modification of data that should stay fixed.
It signals to a reader that the group of values belongs together as one thing, such as a coordinate.

practice.q: A program searches a list of 100,000 student records by ID on every page load and is slow. Explain the cause and suggest an improvement.
points: Searching a list examines each element in turn, so time grows in proportion to the length.
With 100,000 records each lookup may make tens of thousands of comparisons.
Building a dictionary keyed by student ID allows the record to be found directly.
Lookup time then barely changes as the collection grows, at the cost of the memory the dictionary occupies.

practice.q: A function is written to calculate a total and also prints the result and updates a global counter. Discuss why this is poor design.
points: The function does three unrelated things, so its name cannot describe it accurately.
Printing means it cannot be used anywhere the output is unwanted, such as inside another calculation.
Updating a global makes the result depend on, and affect, state outside the function.
It cannot be tested by simply checking its return value, since its effects are elsewhere.
It should return the total and leave printing and counting to the caller, so each responsibility sits in one place.

pages.title: Objects and classes
pages.lede: What an object actually is in memory, why a class is a blueprint rather than a thing, and where every beginner's confusion about self comes from.

cards.a: A single thing in a program that bundles **state** — the data it holds — with **behaviour** — the operations it can perform on that data.
A blueprint describing what every object of that kind has and can do. The class is written once; objects are made from it at run time.
Creating an object from a class, which allocates memory for that object's own attributes and runs the constructor.
A variable belonging to an object, holding part of its state. Two objects of the same class have the same attribute names and their own separate values.
A function that belongs to a class and operates on an object's own data. It is stored once with the class, not copied into every object.
The method that runs when an object is created. It sets the starting values of the attributes, so no object ever exists in a half-built state.
The object the method was called on. It is how a method reaches its own object's data, and it is why `self.name` and a plain local `name` are different things.

cards.q: What is the difference between a class variable and an instance variable?
cards.a: An instance variable belongs to one object and each object has its own. A class variable is shared by every object of that class, so changing it changes it for all of them.
A method that belongs to the class but does not use any object's data. It is called on the class itself and takes no `self`.

cards.q: Why is an object more than a dictionary of values?
cards.a: Because the operations travel with the data. Anything holding the object also holds the only code allowed to change it, so the rules cannot be bypassed.

cards.q: What does it mean to say two variables reference the same object?
cards.a: Both names hold the same address, so there is only one object. A change made through either name is visible through both.

cards.q: What is the difference between identity and equality?
cards.a: Identity asks whether two names point at the *same* object. Equality asks whether two objects hold the same values. Two different objects can be equal.

practice.q: Explain the relationship between a class and an object, using an example.
points: A class is a definition or blueprint stating what attributes and methods objects of that kind have.
An object is a specific instance created from that class at run time.
Each object has its own values for the attributes, so two objects of the same class can differ.
A valid example is given, such as a Student class with objects for individual students.

practice.q: State what a constructor is and explain why it is useful.
points: A constructor is a method that runs automatically when an object is created.
It assigns initial values to the object's attributes.
This guarantees the object is in a valid state before any other code can use it.

practice.q: Distinguish between an instance variable and a class variable, giving a use for each.
points: An instance variable belongs to a single object, and each object has its own copy.
A class variable is shared by every object of the class.
An instance variable suits data that differs per object, such as a student's name.
A class variable suits data common to all objects, such as a count of how many have been created.

practice.q: Explain what is meant by `self` in a method definition and why it is needed.
points: `self` refers to the particular object on which the method was called.
Methods are stored once with the class rather than copied into each object.
The parameter therefore tells the method which object's data to work on.
Without it, an assignment inside the method would create a local variable rather than change the object.

practice.q: A program creates two objects of the same class and changes an attribute of one. Explain why the other is unaffected, and state one case in which it would be affected.
points: Each object has its own memory holding its own instance variables.
Assigning to one object's attribute writes only to that object's storage.
If the attribute were a class variable, it would be shared and both would change.
The same happens if both names reference the same single object rather than two objects.

practice.q: A student writes a program using two parallel lists, one of names and one of marks, and is told to rewrite it using objects. Discuss the advantages of doing so.
points: Related data is held together in one object rather than spread across separate lists.
It becomes impossible for the lists to fall out of step, which is a common source of bugs.
Operations on a student, such as calculating a grade, can be methods on the object rather than loose functions.
Adding a further field requires changing one class rather than every place a list is indexed.
The program reads in terms of the problem — students and marks — rather than in terms of indices.

practice.q: Explain the difference between testing identity and testing equality for objects, and give a situation where the distinction matters.
points: Identity tests whether two references point to the same object in memory.
Equality tests whether two objects hold values that are considered the same.
Two distinct objects can be equal, so an identity test would wrongly report them as different.
It matters when, for example, checking whether a student appears twice in a list, where equality of the data is what is wanted.

pages.title: Encapsulation and interfaces
pages.lede: Why hiding data is not about secrecy, what an invariant is, and how to tell a useful getter from a pointless one.

cards.a: Keeping an object's data private and exposing only methods, so the object's state can only be changed in ways the class allows.
Accessible from anywhere. Anything public is a promise you must keep working, because other code now depends on it.
Accessible only from inside the class. It can be renamed, retyped or removed without breaking any other code.
Accessible from inside the class and from its subclasses, but not from unrelated code.

cards.q: What is an accessor, or getter?
cards.a: A method that returns the value of a private attribute without allowing it to be changed.

cards.q: What is a mutator, or setter?
cards.a: A method that changes a private attribute, and which can validate the new value before accepting it.
A statement about an object that must be true at all times, such as a balance never being negative. Encapsulation is how it is enforced.
Validation happens in one place so bad state cannot be created, and the internal representation can be changed without altering any calling code.

cards.q: What is an interface, in object-oriented terms?
cards.a: The set of public methods an object offers — what it can be asked to do, with nothing said about how it does it.

cards.q: Why is a getter-and-setter pair for every attribute a poor design?
cards.a: Because it exposes the same state under a longer name. Nothing is protected and the class has no rules of its own.
By convention. A leading underscore means "internal", and a double underscore triggers name mangling, but neither is enforced by the language.

cards.q: What does information hiding buy you when a program changes?
cards.a: Anything hidden can be rewritten freely. Only what was exposed constrains you, so a small public interface keeps future options open.

practice.q: Explain what encapsulation is and state two benefits of it.
points: Encapsulation means keeping an object's data private and providing access only through its methods.
Any change to the state must pass through code the class controls.
Validation can therefore be written once and cannot be bypassed.
The internal representation can be changed without affecting code that uses the object.

practice.q: Describe the difference between public, private and protected access.
points: Public members can be accessed from anywhere in the program.
Private members can be accessed only from within the class that defines them.
Protected members can be accessed within the class and its subclasses, but not from unrelated code.

practice.q: A class stores a bank balance as a public attribute. Explain the risks and describe how encapsulation would remove them.
points: Any code anywhere can assign to the balance, including invalid values such as a negative amount.
A wrong value could originate anywhere in the program, making the fault hard to locate.
Making the attribute private and providing deposit and withdraw methods forces all changes through one place.
Those methods can reject invalid amounts, so the object can never enter an invalid state.

practice.q: Explain what is meant by an invariant, and how a class maintains one.
points: An invariant is a condition about an object's state that must always hold.
The constructor establishes it when the object is created.
Every method that changes the state must leave it true, rejecting changes that would break it.
This is only possible if the state cannot be changed from outside the class.

practice.q: A student adds a getter and a setter for every private attribute in a class. Discuss whether this achieves encapsulation.
points: The attributes are technically private, so the syntax of encapsulation is present.
A setter that accepts any value provides the same freedom as a public attribute.
No validation or rule is enforced, so invalid states are still reachable.
Genuine encapsulation means exposing operations that make sense for the object, not exposing every field.

practice.q: Explain how encapsulation makes a program easier to change, referring to the idea of an interface.
points: The public methods form the interface, which is what other code depends on.
Anything private is not depended upon and may be altered freely.
The internal storage could be replaced entirely while the interface stays the same.
Callers therefore continue to work without modification, so the change is contained within the class.

practice.q: A team is designing a Student class. Discuss how they should decide which members are public and which are private.
points: Start by identifying the operations other code genuinely needs to perform on a student.
Those operations become the public interface, expressed in terms of the problem rather than the storage.
Data that has rules attached, such as a mark that must lie between 0 and 100, should be private with validated access.
Anything only needed internally, such as a cached calculation, should be private so it can later be changed or removed.
The default should be private, because making something public later is easy but withdrawing it is not.

pages.title: Inheritance and polymorphism
pages.lede: Reusing a class by extending it, replacing one behaviour without touching the rest, and the reason a list of different things can be treated as one.

cards.a: Defining a class in terms of an existing one, so it gains that class's attributes and methods and adds or replaces what it needs.

cards.q: What are the two classes in an inheritance relationship called?
cards.a: The **superclass**, base or parent, and the **subclass**, derived or child.

cards.q: What relationship must hold for inheritance to be appropriate?
cards.a: **is-a**. A Dog is an Animal. If the sentence is false, inheritance is the wrong tool.
A subclass providing its own version of a method the superclass already defines. Calls on that subclass run the new version.
Objects of different classes responding to the same call in their own way, so one piece of code works with all of them.
The decision about which behaviour to run is made by the object's own type, not by a branch listing every case.
A class that cannot be instantiated, existing to define a common interface and shared behaviour for its subclasses.
A method declared without an implementation, which every concrete subclass must provide.

cards.q: What is composition, and how does it differ from inheritance?
cards.a: Building a class from objects of other classes — **has-a** rather than **is-a**. It is more flexible, because the parts can be swapped at run time.
Behaviour is scattered across many levels, so understanding one method means reading the whole chain, and a change high up affects everything below.

cards.q: What does it mean to call the superclass version of a method?
cards.a: Running the parent's implementation from inside the override, usually to extend it rather than replace it. In Python this is `super()`.

cards.q: What is the Liskov substitution principle, informally?
cards.a: Anywhere the superclass works, a subclass must work too. If a subclass breaks a promise the superclass made, the inheritance is wrong.

practice.q: Explain what inheritance is and state two benefits of using it.
points: A subclass is defined in terms of an existing superclass and automatically has its attributes and methods.
Shared code is written once in the superclass rather than repeated in each subclass.
A change to the shared behaviour is made in one place and applies everywhere.
Subclasses can be treated as instances of the superclass, so common code can process them together.

practice.q: Explain what method overriding is and why a subclass might do it.
points: Overriding means a subclass defines a method with the same name as one in its superclass.
Calls on objects of the subclass use the subclass's version.
It allows a subclass to specialise behaviour that differs from the general case while inheriting everything else.

practice.q: Explain what polymorphism is, using an example, and state why it reduces the need for conditional statements.
points: Polymorphism means objects of different classes respond to the same method call in their own way.
A valid example is given, such as calling `speak()` on a list containing dogs and cats.
The correct version is selected by the type of the object at run time.
The calling code therefore needs no branch listing each possible type, and requires no change when a new type is added.

practice.q: Distinguish between inheritance and composition, and state when each is appropriate.
points: Inheritance models an is-a relationship, where the subclass is a kind of the superclass.
Composition models a has-a relationship, where an object holds other objects as parts.
Inheritance is appropriate when subclasses genuinely satisfy everything promised by the superclass.
Composition is appropriate when behaviour is being reused without such a relationship, and it allows the part to be replaced at run time.

practice.q: Explain what an abstract class is and why one might be used.
points: An abstract class cannot itself be instantiated.
It defines methods that subclasses must implement, and may provide shared implementations of others.
It guarantees that every subclass offers a common interface, so they can be used interchangeably.
It prevents the creation of an object of a general type that has no meaningful concrete behaviour.

practice.q: A developer creates a class Square that inherits from Rectangle and overrides the setters so that width and height are always equal. Discuss whether this is a sound use of inheritance.
points: Mathematically a square is a rectangle, so the is-a test appears to be satisfied.
Code written for a rectangle may assume that setting the width leaves the height unchanged.
A Square breaks that assumption, so it cannot safely be used everywhere a Rectangle can.
This violates the principle that a subclass must be substitutable for its superclass.
A reasoned alternative is given, such as making both immutable, or using a common Shape interface rather than inheriting.

practice.q: Explain why a deep inheritance hierarchy can make a program harder to maintain.
points: Behaviour of one object is defined across several classes, so understanding it means reading the whole chain.
It is not obvious from a subclass which version of a method will actually run.
A change to a class high in the hierarchy affects every class beneath it, possibly unintentionally.
Subclasses become tightly coupled to their parents' implementations, so those cannot be changed freely.

pages.title: Designing with objects
pages.lede: Turning a written problem into classes, reading a UML diagram, and knowing which relationship line to draw between two boxes.

cards.q: What is a UML class diagram?
cards.a: A standard drawing of the classes in a system: a box per class with its attributes and methods, and lines showing how the classes relate.

cards.q: What are the three compartments of a UML class box?
cards.a: The class name, the attributes, and the methods.

cards.q: What do `+` and `−` mean in a UML class box?
cards.a: `+` marks a public member, `−` a private one, and `#` a protected one.
A plain line: one class knows about another and can use it, with no ownership implied.

cards.q: What is aggregation, and how is it drawn?
cards.a: A has-a relationship where the parts can exist without the whole. An open diamond at the whole's end.

cards.q: What is composition, and how is it drawn?
cards.a: A stronger has-a where the parts are owned and die with the whole. A filled diamond at the whole's end.
A line with a hollow triangle pointing at the superclass.
The numbers on the ends of a relationship saying how many objects take part — `1`, `0..1`, `1..*` or `*`.

cards.q: What is a useful first step in identifying classes from a problem description?
cards.a: Underline the nouns as candidate classes and the verbs as candidate methods, then discard the ones that are not worth modelling.

cards.q: What is meant by a class having a single responsibility?
cards.a: It does one job, so there is only one kind of change that would require it to be rewritten.
How much one class depends on the internals of another. Loose coupling means a class can be changed without disturbing its neighbours.
How closely the parts of a class belong together. High cohesion means everything in the class serves its one job.

practice.q: Describe the information shown in a UML class diagram.
points: Each class is drawn as a box divided into name, attributes and methods.
Visibility is shown by symbols such as + for public and − for private.
Lines between boxes show relationships such as association, aggregation, composition and inheritance.
Multiplicities on the line ends show how many objects participate in each relationship.

practice.q: Explain the difference between aggregation and composition, giving an example of each.
points: Both are has-a relationships in which one class holds objects of another.
In aggregation the parts can exist independently of the whole.
In composition the parts belong to the whole and are destroyed with it.
Valid examples are given, such as a team aggregating players, and a book composed of pages.

practice.q: A school library system must let members borrow and return books, and produce a list of overdue loans. Identify four suitable classes and justify one of them.
points: Sensible classes are identified, such as Member, Book, Loan and Library.
Each corresponds to a distinct thing in the problem with its own data.
A justification is given, for example that a Loan has its own attributes such as the date due, so it cannot simply be a field of Book.
The operations of the system map onto methods of these classes.

practice.q: Explain what is meant by high cohesion and why it is desirable.
points: A class has high cohesion when everything in it contributes to a single, clearly stated responsibility.
Such a class is easier to name, understand and test.
Only one kind of requirement change forces it to be rewritten, so changes stay contained.

practice.q: Explain what is meant by coupling, and describe how it can be reduced between two classes.
points: Coupling is the degree to which one class depends on another.
Tight coupling occurs when one class relies on another's internal data or implementation.
Reducing coupling means depending only on a small public interface.
The other class can then be changed or replaced without altering the first.

practice.q: A student designs a single class, GameManager, that holds the board, the players, the scores, the rules and the display code. Discuss the problems with this design and how it should be improved.
points: The class has many unrelated responsibilities, so it has low cohesion.
Any change to the display, the rules or the scoring requires editing the same class, increasing the risk of breaking unrelated behaviour.
It cannot be tested in parts, because the game logic cannot be exercised without the display.
It should be split into classes such as Board, Player, Rules and Display, each with one responsibility.
The manager then coordinates those objects, depending only on their public interfaces.

practice.q: Explain how identifying nouns and verbs in a problem statement helps in designing classes, and state one limitation of the technique.
points: Nouns suggest candidate classes or attributes, since they name things in the problem domain.
Verbs suggest candidate methods, since they name things that can be done.
It provides a systematic starting point rather than requiring the design to be invented from nothing.
A limitation is that it over-produces, since many nouns are attributes or irrelevant, so the list must be filtered by judgement.

pages.title: Abstract data types
pages.lede: The difference between what a structure promises and how it is built, and why an array and a linked list are good at opposite things.

cards.q: What is an abstract data type?
cards.a: A description of the values a structure holds and the operations it supports, with nothing said about how it is stored.

cards.q: What is the difference between an ADT and a data structure?
cards.a: The ADT is the promise — push, pop, isEmpty. The data structure is the implementation that keeps it, such as an array or linked nodes.

cards.q: Why is separating the two useful?
cards.a: Code written against the operations keeps working when the storage is replaced, so the implementation can be changed for performance without rewriting callers.

cards.q: What is a static data structure?
cards.a: One whose size is fixed when it is created, such as an array. Memory is allocated once and cannot grow.

cards.q: What is a dynamic data structure?
cards.a: One that grows and shrinks while the program runs, allocating memory for each element as it is needed.

cards.q: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of a static structure.
cards.a: Access by index is immediate because the address can be calculated. But the size must be guessed in advance, wasting memory or running out.

cards.q: Why can an array be indexed in constant time?
cards.a: Elements are the same size and stored consecutively, so the address is $\text{base} + \text{index} \times \text{size}$ — one calculation regardless of length.

cards.q: What does it cost to insert at the front of an array?
cards.a: Every existing element must be shifted up one place, so the work is proportional to the length of the array.

cards.q: What is a record, or struct?
cards.a: A group of named fields of possibly different types, treated as one value. It is the building block for the node of a dynamic structure.

cards.q: What is a pointer or reference?
cards.a: A value holding the address of something else. It is what allows a node to link to another node held anywhere in memory.

cards.q: Name four common abstract data types.
cards.a: Stack, queue, list, and tree. A set, a map and a graph are also ADTs.

cards.q: How do you choose a data structure?
cards.a: By which operations the program performs most: indexing, inserting in the middle, searching, or taking from the ends.

practice.q: Explain what is meant by an abstract data type, and distinguish it from a data structure.
points: An ADT specifies the data it holds and the operations that may be performed on it.
It says nothing about how the data is physically stored.
A data structure is a concrete implementation, such as an array or a set of linked nodes.
The same ADT can therefore be implemented by more than one data structure.

practice.q: Explain why separating an ADT from its implementation is useful when a program must be maintained.
points: Code that uses the ADT depends only on its operations.
The implementation can be replaced without changing any calling code.
A structure can therefore be swapped for a faster one if performance becomes a problem.
Faults in the implementation are confined to one place rather than spread through the program.

practice.q: Compare static and dynamic data structures.
points: A static structure has a size fixed when it is created; a dynamic one grows and shrinks at run time.
A static structure allocates one block of memory, allowing an element's address to be calculated directly.
A dynamic structure allocates memory per element, so it uses only what is needed but stores a pointer with each element.
A static structure may waste memory or overflow if the size is guessed wrongly, which a dynamic one avoids.

practice.q: Explain why an element of an array can be accessed in constant time.
points: Every element occupies the same number of bytes.
Elements are stored consecutively, so the address is the base address plus the index times the element size.
The calculation takes the same time regardless of the index or the length of the array.

practice.q: A program repeatedly inserts new values at the front of a collection of 10,000 items. Explain why an array performs poorly and what should be used instead.
points: Inserting at the front of an array requires every existing element to be moved up one position.
Each insertion therefore costs work proportional to the number of items, around 10,000 moves.
A linked list inserts at the front by creating a node and changing one pointer.
This takes the same short time regardless of how many items are already stored.

practice.q: Explain what a pointer is and why dynamic data structures depend on them.
points: A pointer holds the memory address of another item of data.
Nodes in a dynamic structure are allocated separately and are not adjacent in memory.
Each node therefore stores a pointer to the next, which is what connects them into a structure.
Following pointers is how the structure is traversed, and rearranging them is how it is modified.

practice.q: A team must store a school's 1,200 student records. Discuss which data structure they should choose, given that records are looked up by ID far more often than they are added or removed.
points: The dominant operation is lookup by a key, not insertion or traversal in order.
Searching a list or array of 1,200 records examines up to 1,200 entries per lookup.
A hash table or dictionary keyed by student ID finds a record in roughly constant time.
A sorted array with binary search is an alternative, costing about eleven comparisons, but insertions then require shifting.
A justified conclusion is reached, noting the extra memory a hash table uses is a reasonable price given the access pattern.

pages.title: Stacks and queues
pages.lede: Two structures defined by what they refuse to let you do, and the reason both turn up everywhere from undo buttons to printers.

cards.a: A collection where items are added and removed at the same end. **Last in, first out**.
`push` adds to the top, `pop` removes and returns the top, `peek` or `top` looks without removing, and `isEmpty` reports whether anything is there.
A collection where items are added at the rear and removed from the front. **First in, first out**.
`enqueue` adds at the rear, `dequeue` removes and returns the front, `peek` looks at the front, and `isEmpty` reports whether anything is there.
Pushing onto a stack that has no room left. In a program it usually means uncontrolled recursion.
Popping from an empty stack. The operation must be refused rather than returning nonsense.

cards.q: Give three uses of a stack.
cards.a: The call stack for function calls, undo history, and evaluating expressions or matching brackets.

cards.q: Give three uses of a queue.
cards.a: A print spooler, keystrokes waiting to be processed, and packets buffered at a router.

cards.q: What is a circular queue and why is it used?
cards.a: A fixed array in which the front and rear indices wrap round with modulo. It reuses freed space without shifting elements down.

cards.q: Why not implement a queue as an array with the front always at index 0?
cards.a: Every dequeue would shift all remaining elements one place, making removal cost work proportional to the length.
A queue where each item has a priority and the highest-priority item leaves first, regardless of arrival order.

cards.q: How do you tell a full circular queue from an empty one?
cards.a: Both give `front == rear`, so either keep a count of items or leave one slot always unused.

practice.q: Describe the operations of a stack and state the order in which items are removed.
points: push adds an item to the top of the stack.
pop removes and returns the item at the top.
peek returns the top item without removing it, and isEmpty tests whether the stack holds anything.
Items are removed in the reverse of the order they were added, which is last in, first out.

practice.q: Explain the difference between a stack and a queue, giving one appropriate use of each.
points: A stack adds and removes at the same end, so the most recently added item leaves first.
